November Mini GT Preorder Reveals Six Fast Cars: One of Them Is a New Casting!
20 photos
Photo: MINI GT
I’ve been trying to dive deeper into the stories of various diecast manufacturers for over a year now. After Mattel’s Hot Wheels line I explored what Tarmac Works is all about, and I don’t want to stop there. I’ve got Greenlight and Mini GT on my agenda, but finding the right window for an interview seems to be quite complicated.
I guess it will happen sooner or rather if I keep pushing for a meeting. Unboxing the company’s products can only take you so far, and online research almost never answers all the questions. Maybe I should try to get a hold of Jun Imai next, especially since I’ve started spending more time looking a Kaido House collectibles in recent months.
Anyway, I was somewhat surprised to see a new pre-order post from Mini GT today. I thought to myself: “Didn’t we just have one recently?” Then I started connecting the dots and realized that we get a new selection of cars every two weeks. It’s typically a line-up of six collectibles, but we have had seven of them on the menu twice recently.
This predictable launch pattern works great if you ask me. You just need to find the patience required for pre-order items to be delivered from the factory. I only signed up for the first one a few months ago I believe, which means I should be able to enjoy the cars shortly. Alas, let’s focus on this first release for November.
There’s only one brand-new casting inside, and I’m thrilled to see it given I just recently reviewed NASCAR 26 on my PS5 . You might recognize the #24 Next Gen Garage 56 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 that raced at the 2023 24hrs of Le Mans. This was a modified version of a Cup Series car, that Jenson Button, Jimmie Johnson and Mike Rockenfeller drove for 285 laps at the iconic event.
Photo: MINI GT They ultimately finished P39 out of 62 cars on the grid. It’s worth mentioning, however, that only 40 cars actually finished the race. Given my chronic nostalgia, I’d probably order one of these if it was a replica of a Gen 4 car instead as I’m still mentally stuck on motorsports from that day and age.
Anyway, I’m sure this new casting opens up a long list of opportunities for future variations, considering the Next Gen cars have been around since 2022. This is the only American car on the list for today, as the other five machines will take us over to the old continent.
While I acknowledge that the BMW M4 GT3 EVO is quite cool, it’s not nearly as exciting as the Lamborghini Huracan GT3 EVO2. I’m not familiar with either the two teams running these in their program, and that’s great.
What Mini GT is doing (and I’ve seen this with Tarmac Works as well) is highlighting projects that take us away from the “hype zone” into a zone where we can learn more about motorsports and the history of racing from the comfort of our living room. The other BMW in this pre-order is a bit more relaxed, although certainly not short on power.
Photo: MINI GT I can’t recall exactly when the BMW M5 debuted, but I’m almost certain it sported the now iconic Isle of Man Green Metallic finish. There’s also an Alpine White version of the sedan to look for, plus a few iterations of the M5 Touring model . It’s the only item on the list where you can choose between a LHD or RHD model, which is one feature I don’t remember seeing any other 1/64th-scale manufacturer offering.
Now that we’re done with Germany, let’s move over to the United Kingdom for the Jaguar C-X75 and the Aston Martin Valkyrie. Right off the bat, I can think of five previous variations for the Jag and I’m almost certain the Spectre replica has been the most desired one so far. It’s a car that deserves bright colors, which is my take for most of the machines that have an identity built around speed.
I’m aware different people will have different opinions on the topic, which is why I don’t believe that the new version of the Jag can become a peg-warmer. The Valkyrie was also available in the previous pre-order. I didn’t like the Escaping White finish, and I’m not a fan of Cobalt Blue either.
Hyper Red, Sunburst Yellow, Maximum Orange and Aston Martin Racing Green were available before, and the Chase variations are the only ones that might “hurt” your bank account. I’m not even talking Hot Wheels Super Treasure Hunt figures here, so don’t worry about it.
As always, the pre-order window is only open for a relatively short period. And signing up for one (or all) of these means you’ll have to wait until Q2 of 2027 to have them delivered to your place. Until then, the market has plenty of readily-available options to choose from.

As part of those energy affordability considerations, conversations and proposals are increasingly contemplating who should be allowed to own the batteries that keep the grid running. Utilities, independent developers and customer-owned systems can all deliver various grid services. The states that let all three compete for the same projects tend to land the lowest prices for ratepayers. The states that restrict or prioritize a singular ownership model run the risk of higher rates for ratepayers.
That is the caution regulators should carry into every storage docket: a policy that favors utility ownership over private developers, or the reverse, trades a competitive market for a guaranteed one, and someone always ends up covering the difference. Minnesota’s newest battery program shows what that looks like when that caution goes missing.
COMMENTARY
The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved a plan this year letting the utility own up to 200 megawatts of batteries, backed by a $430 million budget. Third-party developers never got the chance to compete for that same work.
MnSEIA, SEIA, and the Coalition for Community Solar Access say the plan shifts financial risk onto ratepayers while shutting out cheaper third-party ownership alternatives. SEIA calls it the only utility-owned virtual power plant of its kind in the country with a cost-benefit ratio below one. Ratepayers will be forced to cover that gap regardless of how the batteries perform.
This math traces back to how utility regulation works. A regulated utility earns a fixed return on whatever capital it invests. A bigger, costlier battery system earns a bigger return than a cheaper one that solves the same grid problem. An ownership target locks that price in because no competing bid ever gets the chance to challenge it.
States already have a model for setting targets well. A renewable portfolio standard sets a target for how much clean energy the grid needs. It does not name who has to own the plants that supply it. Utilities, independent developers or co-ops can all vie to meet that goal.
A utility-ownership target or incentive for storage breaks that pattern. It names the owner before anyone else can bid on price or performance.
Encore Renewable Energy owns and operates a portfolio of battery projects in Vermont, with dozens of other projects in development in New York, Illinois and Colorado. Utilities pay for predictable peak-load reduction: they predict the load events, and the batteries discharge accordingly to manage the most challenging and expensive hours of demand. Revenue is also generated from other services the battery performs, like energy arbitrage and ancillary services, markets a rate-based utility battery cannot enter, since its return already comes through the rate base.
If there are unexpected costs or performance issues, the independent owner absorbs that cost, not the ratepayers. It never reaches a customer’s power bill. Private capital takes on that risk so ratepayers do not have to.
Pricing structures can vary as much as ownership does. Some contracts pay the developer for performance, the way Encore’s Vermont projects do. Others use a fixed-fee model instead: the utility takes all the project’s revenue and pays the developer one set amount, while the developer still owns the asset and carries its performance and technology risk. Either approach can pair with any ownership structure. Deal terms and who owns the asset are separate questions, each with more than one fair answer.
None of this shuts out utilities. They still have a real operational role. Coordinating thousands of small batteries sitting behind customers’ meters, and calling on that combined capacity when the grid needs it, puts a utility in position to act at a scale no single developer can match. The batteries themselves can still belong to the customers or developers who installed them.
The same holds for grid maintenance: utilities keep the poles and wires running and respond when a storm knocks out power across a county, better than any developer could. None of that requires owning the batteries that support it.
States can fix the ownership-target problem by setting a target for total storage capacity and requiring every project to win that capacity through competitive bidding (with utilities included in the bidding).
New Hampshire just expanded utility-ownership authority in a similar way, though its new law points at gas and nuclear plants rather than batteries. The new law lets utilities own up to 10% of their peak load in new generation, with no single unit larger than 5 megawatts.
The bill drew similar objections around energy affordability; it shifts financial risk onto ratepayers and narrows a competitive market before competition can start.
Let utilities run the grid they know how to run. Let private developers take on the risk they know how to manage, and let price decide who builds what. That’s what keeps energy affordable, and it’s the standard every state’s storage policy should be measured against.
—Chad Farrell is founder and president of Encore Renewable Energy , a Vermont-based developer and owner/operator of solar and energy storage projects across the U.S.

Vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.
But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.
Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.
The biggest upgrade is an entirely new electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
On the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa says the new motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.
But perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the new removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.
The Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.
Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.
There’s also a new charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.
The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.
Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole update is how little of it you can actually see.
The company hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.
Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the new models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

What happens if a battery energy storage system (BESS) falls below its guaranteed capacity in year six? The owner negotiated the performance guarantee seven years ago, and that performance guarantee may be set in the Supply Agreement or it may be set in the Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA). More and more original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are looking to push, or indeed have already pushed, the performance guarantee into the LTSA.
The consequence of that shortfall was papered years earlier, when the equipment was selected and the supply and service contracts were negotiated. It is the supply contract that determines what happens when equipment is late, performance falls short, a component fails, the system needs augmentation, or the OEM can no longer support the product.
That is where commercial due diligence becomes critical. It is an assessment of how the project agreements work together, where the material risks sit, and whether the protections and remedies in those agreements support the project’s financing, operating requirements, and long-term value.
Where the Liability Actually Sits
Project owners change, people move to new companies, and as a result, owners need to dig to find out which contract applies when those guarantees are missed, or what the limit of liability is capped at in those instances. During the initial defect and workmanship warranty period, typically the first two years, most OEMs offer a bumper-to-bumper type warranty. Equipment failing for reasons attributable to the manufacturer is repaired or replaced, and the limitation of liability under the supply agreement generally extends to the full contract price. That is meaningful protection, and it is usually the protection owners have in mind when they describe their warranty position to a lender.
What the warranty frequently omits is any commitment to a response or repair time. A system sitting below guaranteed performance while it waits for repair is not accounted for by the warranty at all. That shortfall often falls to availability liquidated damages under the LTSA, where the limit of liability is usually much lower, commonly one to three times the annual service fee.
From year three onward, the LTSA is often the only contract addressing performance problems, even though the performance guarantee itself runs for the full contracted life of the system, usually 20 years. Some OEMs place damages for lost MWh under the supply agreement, others under the LTSA. Owners need to know which applies, how damages are calculated, and what cap on damages exists in each case.
The cumulative arithmetic is what makes this a bankability question. An aggregate LTSA cap can become an event of default through shortfalls across two or three consecutive years. Beyond that point, the contractual incentive for the manufacturer to restore guaranteed performance is substantially reduced.
How Commercial Risk Affects Financing
The potential consequence of an inadequate remedy does not wait until year six. It arrives during diligence, when lenders and other financing partners evaluate whether the agreements sufficiently address operating and financial requirements.
Financing parties underwrite the downside case. Where the documents leave uncertainty about who absorbs a performance shortfall, or where the available remedy is visibly smaller than the exposure it covers, the risk will affect financing assumptions and project economics. Collectively, those risks reduce leverage, raise the cost of capital, and take value out of the investor’s return.
That is the practical meaning of “bankability” or “financeability” in this case. The objective is to identify material risks before financing and procurement decisions are finalized, determine which party is best positioned to manage them, and make clear what exposure remains with the project owner.
The Seams Between Contracts
BESS projects (Figure 1) run on a contract structure covering equipment supply, procurement and construction, commissioning, warranties, and the LTSA, along with offtake and interconnection agreements that establish many of a project’s operating requirements. Commercial due diligence needs to determine whether the obligations, performance requirements, and remedies stay aligned when those agreements are considered together.
1. Battery energy storage system, or BESS, projects run on a contract structure covering equipment supply, procurement and construction, warranties, and service agreements, along with other issues such as offtake and interconnection agreements. Courtesy: Invera Energy
The common approach is to create “one throat to choke” with the BESS supplier responsible for inverter and transformer performance, along with the batteries. This can reduce uncertainty over responsibility when a performance issue involves equipment from multiple suppliers. In some cases, EPC contractors are made the initial purchaser of the BESS to keep delivery aligned with construction milestones. In this case, the project owner stays fully engaged in those negotiations, because terms agreed during that negotiation will govern the asset for two decades.
Other contract provisions can have consequences beyond the supplier relationship. Many suppliers, for example, restrict assignment to transfer to competitors. Depending on how competitor is defined, that restriction can complicate financing or a later sale.
Evolving federal requirements add another layer to commercial risk allocation. Foreign entity of concern (FEOC) requirements can affect tax credit eligibility and require greater visibility into supplier ownership, manufacturing and sourcing. Owners should understand what information the OEM is required to provide, what happens if sourcing or manufacturing strategies change, and how future regulatory changes will be addressed. While an OEM may not accept responsibility for project-level tax credit qualification, the project owner should not be left to carry the entire risk while relying on information controlled by the supplier.
Lastly, tariff allocation presents a different type of commercial risk. Many BESS supply contracts now include tariff-sharing mechanisms. An OEM may assume responsibility for changes within an agreed collar around the starting tariff, with the buyer taking the risk outside that collar. If tariffs exceed an agreed-upon level, either party has the ability to terminate the agreement. The appropriate structure will depend on the project, yet the owner needs to understand the potential exposure and how it has been allocated before signing.
A 20-Year Partnership, Signed on Day One
A supply agreement opens a two-decade relationship in which the owner depends on the OEM for service, software, source code, technical documentation, specialized knowledge, and spare parts. Owners must account for the possibility, and real risk, that an OEM may exit the market, become insolvent, or discontinue support for a particular product.
That must be addressed during negotiations of the original supply agreement. An intellectual property, or IP, escrow can protect access to source code and documentation, owner step-in rights, and the ability to engage qualified third-party service providers, in case of project abandonment. Where the long-term plan involves self-performing a certain scope, it is recommended to include training and the right to terminate early in the LTSA. Without those rights, a functioning asset becomes harder to maintain, harder to finance, and harder to sell.
Augmentation, Decided Now and Delivered Later
For projects anticipating future augmentation, the commercial strategy belongs in the initial procurement process, even where the additional equipment may not be required for a decade. There are broadly two approaches, and they place the future risk differently.
The first incorporates augmentation into the original supply agreement, obligating the OEM to maintain a specified energy capacity at the point of measurement, or POM, throughout the term. The pricing risk will then either be taken outright by the OEM or shared with the buyer through a cap on pricing.
The second approach leaves the augmentation obligation and its pricing risk with the owner. This option requires the project owner to plan for available space, hardware, and software compatibility, and the effect of augmentation costs on returns.
Under either approach, the original agreement should establish how warranties and performance guarantees operate after augmentation. Those questions are easier to resolve during initial procurement than years later, when capacity is needed, and the equipment and contracting options available may be considerably fewer.
The Window Closes at Signature
The objective of commercial due diligence is to de-risk project execution by identifying gaps in responsibilities, monitoring contractual obligations, and helping to manage issues before they result in delays or cost overruns. It aims to identify each material risk, allocate it to whichever party is best positioned to manage it, and put a functioning remedy behind whatever remains with the project owner.
Those decisions have a window, and that window closes when equipment is selected and agreements are executed. Afterward, any inconsistency between two contracts or an obligation that no one carried into the operating phase stops being a negotiation and becomes a dispute.
The owner in year six has one question worth asking: What is the guarantee worth? That answer was written years before the shortfall and priced into the financing before the equipment was shipped. Understanding the performance of the chosen technology is the straightforward half of procurement. Knowing who is accountable when the equipment does not perform, or if there is a disruption, and explaining that to the underwriters, is how the decision is made as to whether a project is bankable.
—Terri Denning is president of Invera Energy and an expert in BESS procurement, contracting, and risk management.

General Motors 8.3L Duramax HD Turbo Diesel Truck Production Starts on November 16 at Flint Assembly
17 photos
Photo: Chevrolet
Flint Assembly in Michigan is currently wrapping up Silverado HD and Sierra HD turbo diesel truck production for model year 2026. Starting November 16, the 2027 models with the new Mongoose engine will be rolling off the assembly line.
This information comes from GM Trucks, which underlines that Flint builds the 2500 and 3500 versions of the Silverado HD and Sierra HD, including duallies. Over at General Motors, the Detroit-based automaker says that both 2027 models would launch in the latter part of 2026.
General Motors further assembles HD trucks at its Oshawa facility in Canada. The 8.3-liter Duramax, meanwhile, hails from the DMAX facility in Ohio. Internally referred to as L6P as opposed to L5P for the diesel engine it replaces, the newcomer develops a best-in-segment 555 horsepower. Peak torque is estimated at 1,230 pound-feet (1,668 Newton-meters).
That makes the L6P a lot punchier than its forerunner, which is only natural given the difference in displacement. Opting for the 8.3-liter unit results in another 85 horsepower and 255 pound-feet (346 Newton-meters), figures that unlock slightly higher maximum towing figures.
GM says the L6P is a clean-sheet design. Compared to the standard naturally aspirated small-block V8, which boasts 6.6 liters, the diesel option costs $11,400 for model year 2027 as opposed to $9,900 for its predecessor. The outgoing L5P still has a compelling argument for many customers, giving service technicians a very familiar platform to work on.
Photo: GM New powertrains, especially those developed specifically for towing this much, are way more susceptible to minor and major issues. We also have to remember that Chevy and GMC dealers will be much obliged to get rid of 2026 models by offering end-of-production incentives.
Paired with a 10-speed automatic that carries Allison branding even though it's not a true Allison tranny, said engine is compatible with B20 fuel and uses a compacted graphite iron block. Forged conrods, a forged crank, and forged pistons also need mentioning, along with a variable-geometry turbo, dual stage air-to-water charge cooling, piston-cooling oil jets, a variable-displacement oil pump, and new exhaust after-treatment goodies.
As far as the Silverado HD is concerned, the Chevrolet division lists a maximum available towing capacity of 38,000 pounds (17,237 kilograms). Maximum payload comes in at 6,170 pounds (2,799 kilograms). Downgrading to the 6.6-liter gasoline V8 results in maximum figures of 19,000 and 6,990 pounds, respectively, meaning 8,618 and 3,171 kilograms in metric speak.
L8S is the regular production option code of the gasser, which replaces the L8T in the heavy-duty truck range. Assembled in Tonawanda, New York, this lump generates a very respectable 412 horsepower and 472 pound-feet (640 Newton-meters) of twist on regular unleaded.
Major differences over the L8T include the redesigned intake manifold, which boosts airflow efficiency, an upgraded cooling system that includes a redesigned water pump, new internal oil passages, a different oil pan, and a digital oil level display in the instrument cluster instead of a dipstick. Both mills are joined by rack-and-pinion electric power steering.
For model year 2027, the HD trucks also get an electronic brake-boost system. The final highlights come in the form of updated Tow/Haul and Off-Road modes.

Port and terminal businesses are expanding their use of artificial intelligence , but very few can show it’s adding to earnings, according to a survey from Boston Consulting Group (BCG) and TIC4.0.
What’s Related
Only 4% of respondents said they can point to a measurable earnings gain from AI. Only 11% said they track AI’s contribution systematically.
Forty-four percent of respondents said their organizations are expanding AI beyond early testing. That number rises to 56% at companies with more than $8 billion in revenue and drops to 32% at those under $1 billion.
What's the ROI?
Unclear return on investment topped the list of barriers at 41%. Data quality came next at 32%, followed by connecting existing systems at 30%. Implementation cost and uncertainty about carrying out projects each came in at 28%.
The doubt grows the further you get from the top. Twenty-one percent of C-suite leaders named unclear ROI as a problem, compared with 44% of respondents below the C-suite.
Customers are pushing for AI. Respondents said demand comes mostly from freight forwarders (61%), third-party logistics providers (58%), and container lines (52%). Respondents' benefits are mostly tied to work inside the terminal. Efficiency led at 74%, followed by faster decisions at 44% and cost reduction at 41%. Only 18% cited a better customer experience.
RELATED: Why Port AI Projects Keep Running Into the Same Old Data Problem
Where the money is going
Hiring and training AI talent leads planned spending at 59%. Research and development comes next at 55%, then adding AI modules to existing systems at 47%. Just 2% plan no AI spending at all.
Half of respondents expect workers to be reskilled or moved into new jobs, while 31% expect less demand for labor .
Based on its AI work, BCG estimates that algorithms drive 10% of value creation, technology and data 20% and training and processes 70%.
Four moves for port leaders
The report lays out four steps:
Prove value before scaling . Set baselines and timelines, assign one person to each pilot to own the results, and use go/no-go checkpoints.
Fix data across the whole company. Treat data as shared infrastructure and adopt common industry data standards.
Put AI into everyday terminal work. Focus spending on forecasting and equipment dispatch, and fund employee retraining.
Build commercial services for customers such as forwarders, logistics providers and liners. Examples include cargo visibility and proactive updates.
Over the next year, BCG recommends testing a short list of AI projects against clear measures agreed on with frontline managers. Operators should also improve shared data before expanding AI into more daily tasks.

Pfizer plans to build a $650 million Manufacturing Technology Center at its research and development campus in Groton, Conn., AdvanceCT announced last week.
What’s Related
The roughly 220,000-square-foot facility will manufacture clinical active pharmaceutical ingredients and drug products for Pfizer-sponsored clinical trials worldwide. Construction is set to start in the second quarter of 2027, with operations targeted for mid-2031.
Pfizer will spend $650 million over the next five years, according to AdvanceCT, the state’s nonprofit economic development group.
“Pfizer has a long and proud history of scientific innovation in Groton, where many of the discoveries that advance our pipeline begin. Building on that legacy, the new Manufacturing Technology Center will advance our ability to support clinical research and the development of new medicines for patients around the world,” said Raja Mangipudy, Ph.D., Pfizer’s Groton site head.
Bringing the work under one roof
The project won’t add new jobs . Instead, the center will bring together employees who now work in other buildings across the Groton campus. The project will update the infrastructure behind Pfizer’s current workforce and pull related operations into a new building designed for the company’s future clinical manufacturing needs.
The announcement doesn’t list any state incentives for the project.
The Groton campus covers 175 acres and employs about 2,700 people, according to the Connecticut Business and Industry Association. It has more than 2 million square feet of lab and office space. Pfizer has been in Groton since 1946.
RELATED: Amazon Eyes Second Massive Warehouse in Eastern Connecticut
A major Pfizer research center
Groton is one of Pfizer’s major research centers. The site’s work spans scientific discovery, pharmaceutical sciences, and clinical development, along with the global supply of materials used in clinical research.
“The Manufacturing Technology Center will connect scientific discovery with the advanced manufacturing capabilities needed to support clinical trials around the world,” said John Bourdeaux, president and CEO of AdvanceCT.
State officials called the project a win for Connecticut.
“Pfizer’s investment is an endorsement of the strong momentum across Connecticut’s economy , as companies in a wide range of industries choose to expand , modernize, and make long-term commitments here,” said Daniel O’Keefe, Connecticut’s commissioner of economic development.
Local leaders also welcomed the news.
“This new Manufacturing Technology Center reflects a long-term commitment to our city and the talented people who work here,” said Jill Rusk, mayor of the City of Groton.

For model year 2027, the L8T-replacing L8S is the standard engine in the heavy-duty Silverado and Sierra. Just like the 5.7- and 6.6-liter small blocks of the half-ton pickups, the heavy-duty workhorses with the heavy-duty gasser also drop the dipstick in favor of a sensor with a readout in the digital instrument cluster.
GM Trucks confirmed the switch first, and every trim gets it for model year 2027. Designated L8S in the order guide, the 6.6-liter small block develops a respectable 412 horsepower and 472 pound-feet (640 Newton-meters) of twist. Similar to the preceding L8T, said engine does not come with auto start-stop or dynamic fuel management in the form of cylinder deactivation.
Gifted with an iron block, the L8S differs from the L8T it replaces through an updated oiling system, a less restrictive air intake, a redesigned water pump, and a new oil cooler for good measure. Compared to its forerunner, it develops 11 more horsepower and 8 additional pound-feet.
When it comes to comparisons with the L76 and L78 engines of the half-ton Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, the L8S further differentiates itself through direct injection. Both half-ton truck engines feature dual injection, and the addition of port injection does come with a few advantages over a strictly direct setup. Not only does it eliminate carbon buildup on the intake valves, but it also enables a smoother idle and higher compression without knock.
The digital engine oil level readout may seem convenient, and it surely is. On the other hand, relying on a sensor to monitor engine oil levels isn't as reliable in the long run as a physical dipstick under the hood. Leaving customers dependent on electronics and software for something this basic doesn't sit right with me.
Photo: GM Removing the dipstick feels cheap on the Detroit-based automaker's part, even if the company saves very little money. Looking at the bigger picture, the sensor and digital readout are pricier to produce from the outset than a dipstick and its tube.
Beyond the L8S, prospective customers are further presented with an optional turbo diesel V8 advertised with 8.3 liters to its name. This Duramax is referred to as Mongoose or L6P, and it's a clean-sheet design to boot. A different animal from the L5P it replaces, the 8.3 develops a massive 555 horsepower and 1,230 pound-feet (1,668 Newton-meters) of twist.
Because it's lighter than the Duramax, the gasoline V8 is the better pick for payload. When properly equipped, the Tonawanda-produced engine is much obliged to handle 6,990 pounds (3,171 kilograms) compared to 6,170 (2,799) for the Duramax, which hails from Brookville, Ohio.
Towing, meanwhile, is the specialty of the segment's largest diesel. For model year 2027, the Silverado HD with the L6P is good for up to 38,000 pounds (17,237 kilograms) compared to 19,000 (8,618) for the L8S.

GE Vernova announced on Nov. 6 that it has been officially chosen by PowerGrid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL) to deliver a critical 6-GW High-Voltage Direct-Current (HVDC) transmission corridor. The project was booked in the fourth quarter of 2026.
This project will serve as a vital energy highway, enabling the efficient transport of 6 GW of power from the renewable energy-rich region of Barmer, Rajasthan, to the load center in South Kalamb.
By connecting remote renewable energy zones to the national network, this 800-kV project aims to provide the infrastructure needed to stabilize power flow for millions of homes and businesses. As India’s electricity demand continues to grow, this high-capacity link is essential to ensuring that the country’s grid remains reliable and resilient while supporting its decarbonization goals.
Key Takeaways Project will facilitate the transmission of 6 GW of clean power from the renewable energy zone in Barmer, Rajasthan, to support national energy demand. The project was booked in the fourth quarter of 2026. Reinforces GE Vernova’s commitment to modernizing India’s power system, ensuring greater stability and efficiency for the national grid.
“India is at the forefront of the global energy transition, characterized by an unprecedented scale of renewable integration and rapidly evolving grid requirements,” said Philippe Piron, president and CEO of GE Vernova’s Electrification segment. “This project represents more than just transmission capacity; it is an investment in the reliability and future-proofing of India’s power system. We are proud to work with PGCIL to deploy the advanced technology required to bridge the gap between renewable energy production and national consumption, ensuring long-term system performance.”
“As India accelerates its renewable energy journey, the development of robust, high-capacity transmission infrastructure is paramount,” said Sandeep Zanzaria, CEO and managing director at GE Vernova, T&D India. “The Barmer–South Kalamb HVDC corridor is a strategic project for PGCIL, designed to efficiently integrate large-scale renewable capacity from Rajasthan into the national grid. By leveraging advanced transmission technologies, we are strengthening the backbone of India’s power system, ensuring reliable, high-quality electricity reaches consumers across the country while supporting our national commitment to a sustainable and resilient energy future.”
GE Vernova will deliver the complete design for the ±800-kV, 6,000-MW (2 x 3000-MW) bipolar HVDC link between Barmer II and South Kalamb. The project scope encompasses the creation of new converter stations, the supply of all major equipment, and the full management of site erection, testing, and commissioning. By overseeing the end-to-end delivery of this link, GE Vernova ensures a synchronized approach that prioritizes grid stability and system efficiency, suitable for large-scale renewable energy links such as Barmer.
The project will feature GE Vernova’s most advanced LCC (line commutated converter) valve, which will be manufactured at the Pallavaram factory in India. It will also include the eLumina control system, which provides the digital intelligence required to manage complex power flows, enabling the grid to respond dynamically to changing conditions.
This collaboration further strengthens GE Vernova’s long-standing relationship with PGCIL, reinforcing a shared vision of a modernized, resilient, and decarbonized power grid for the future.
About GE Vernova GE Vernova is a purpose-built global energy company that includes Power, Wind, and Electrification segments and is supported by its accelerator businesses. Building on over 130 years of experience tackling the world’s challenges, GE Vernova is uniquely positioned to help lead the energy transition by continuing to electrify the world while simultaneously working to decarbonize it. GE Vernova helps customers power economies and deliver electricity that is vital to health, safety, security, and improved quality of life. GE Vernova is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, U.S., with more than 75,000 employees across 100+ countries.

Subaru China Recalls Nearly 200,000 Older Models Over Wiring Issue
13 photos
Photo: Subaru
As you're well aware, the steering wheel of a modern automobile does a lot more than simply turn the front wheels. It carries a surprisingly large collection of electrical functions, and 'electrical' is the key word here. Per the Subaru brand's latest recall, a guide inside the steering wheel's spiral cable may damage internal wiring.
This failure concerns up to 196,494 imported vehicles in the Chinese market, and such a failure leaves the horn inoperable. According to the recall documentation filed with the State Administration for Market Regulation, the folks at Subaru Automobile expect the campaign to start on December 21, 2026.
S2026M0135I is what Subaru Automobile calls the campaign, which covers BRZ , XV, Outback, Legacy, and Forester models produced from August 23, 2011, through August 25, 2016. Better known as a clock spring or steering roll connector, the subject component is referred to as a spiral cable in the Chinese-market notice.
Its job is pretty straightforward. When the steering wheel rotates, the electrical connections need to link it to the stationary wiring in the steering column. A flexible coiled conductor allows steering wheel movement without forcing regular wires to twist around the column every time someone negotiates a roundabout.
Subaru Automobile highlights that internal guides may lead to an internal failure, which means that said guides cause premature wear of the internal wiring. Most surprisingly, the filing published by the SAMR does not mention associated failures of the steering wheel airbag, power steering, or any other systems.
Photo: Subaru The Japanese automaker has dealt with similar problems before, albeit the older campaigns involved different production dates and componentry. Back in 2010, for example, both the Legacy and Outback were recalled in the US with the blessing of the NHTSA due to steering column roll connectors that could break.
Said condition disables the horn, steering wheel airbag, cruise control switches, radio controls, and the paddle shifters, if equipped. Subaru of America instructed US-market dealers at the time to inspect the connector's production lot number. Suspect connectors were replaced at no charge to affected owners and lessees.
A corresponding recall was published by the Japanese regulator, and its filing identified variations in the grease applied to the roll connector's flat cable. In other words, those connectors were susceptible to breaking due to chemical stress cracks.
Australia has relevant context as well, with Subaru Australia recalling the Impreza, XV, and Forester as part of campaign SRT-215 for wiring that could wear prematurely due to contact with a metal plate inside the steering column surround. The affected circuits included the horn and steering wheel controls. In extreme circumstances, a short could interrupt power to the engine control unit.
Turning our attention back to the Chinese recall, the company will contact affected customers by telephone, SMS, and via WeChat. Those who prefer taking matters into their own hands may contact Subaru Automobile directly or their preferred retailers for more information.

Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.
But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.
A big map, and no cars spotted yet
Tesla’s official Robotaxi account made the announcement just after midnight local time: “Robotaxi available in San Antonio starting tomorrow, 5am.” It came with a map of the “launch geofence,” a large polygon that runs from Loop 1604 on the north side down to just south of downtown.
Robotaxi Tracker , which measures operator maps and logs fleet sightings, puts the zone at 274 square miles. That covers about 1.0 million residents (51% of the metro) and 721,000 jobs. San Antonio International Airport sits inside the polygon, but it isn’t served.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Waymo started driverless rides in San Antonio in February with more than 60 square miles and opened to all riders in October, airport trips included. Robotaxi Tracker currently lists Waymo’s San Antonio area at 59 square miles.
What Tesla didn’t say is how many cars will cover its 274 square miles. As of Monday morning, Robotaxi Tracker hadn’t logged a single Tesla Robotaxi in San Antonio.
The launch landed the same day Tesla expanded Austin again. The tracker now measures Tesla’s Austin zone at 443 square miles, up 178 square miles since mid-September.
The map isn’t the service
We’ve seen this movie. Last month, Tesla expanded its Houston geofence into the shape of a rocket , and within two days the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app refusing downtown pickups inside it .
Since then, Koby Pierce, who tracks Tesla’s service on X, has done the tedious work of checking city after city. He searched thousands of real addresses in the Robotaxi app on an emulator and mapped only the ones where Tesla allows a pickup or drop-off, then compared that with the map Tesla advertises. Here’s the share of Tesla’s advertised land area that actually works:
Austin: about 59% (83% of residents)
Miami: 61% (67% of residents)
Orlando: about 70%
Fort Worth: about 72%
Houston: about 74%
Dallas: 78% (89% of residents)
Austin's dropoff/pickup Geofence is ~41% smaller than advertised. Seems mostly the East side of town is inaccessible. Unsure the cause. Any ideas? Dallas is next and should be done by noon tomrrow. pic.twitter.com/WvU99sJlJh — Koby Pierce (@koby_pierce) November 3, 2026
Austin is the one that matters. It’s Tesla’s flagship market, with 453 unsupervised vehicles in service according to Robotaxi Tracker. Yet about 41% of the advertised map Pierce tested, mostly on the east side of town, wouldn’t take a ride request. Pierce points to railroad crossings as a big factor in several cities, which lines up with the strange downtown routing we saw in Houston.
To be fair, Pierce says Waymo is next on his list, and he expects “they’re no better.” Robotaxi Tracker already had to trim Waymo’s Orlando area last month after finding the airport, inside Waymo’s published map, wasn’t selectable. We’ll look at those numbers when they’re out. But it doesn’t change what Tesla is doing with San Antonio today.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. A 274-square-mile launch in a new city is progress, and Tesla now runs unsupervised rides in eight cities. At the start of this year, it had no unsupervised rides anywhere.
But we need to stop taking Tesla’s geofence numbers at face value, and that includes us. We used Tesla’s 254-square-mile figure for Houston, and it turned out to be overstated. In all six cities Pierce has checked, the real service area is between 59% and 78% of what Tesla posts. In Austin and Miami, it’s about 60%.
So the honest way to read the San Antonio announcement is “up to 274 square miles.” In practice, expect something closer to 160 to 210 square miles, with an unknown number of cars, and the airport already off the table. That’s still bigger than Waymo’s 59 square miles in the city.

And what Electrek missed to report is that in Austin for the first time ever more Cybercabs were on the roads than Waymos. Reported by also an by independent tracker site.
Gradually, then suddenly.

The problem is that square miles are the metric Tesla fully controls. Drawing a polygon costs nothing, and the numbers were all over X within hours of the post. Cars per square mile, wait times, and rides completed are much harder to inflate, and nationally Waymo still runs over 4,000 driverless vehicles to Tesla’s 666, per Robotaxi Tracker.
I still consider this a small pilot by any standard, and safety remains the bottleneck. Tesla is still forcing riders through hour-long rides that should take 15 minutes because they have to take routes that avoid areas that Tesla can’t safely navigate without supervision.
Until that’s fixed, robotaxi won’t be able to meaningfully scale beyond these limited demonstrations in geo-fenced areas.

source_document.body:
When people talk about innovation in energy storage, the conversation usually starts with batteries: chemistry, capacity, and duration. Those areas are important, but they are not the whole system. As energy storage systems move toward higher voltages, higher power, and more compact designs, the components inside them must also handle more demanding electrical conditions.
This changes how components need to be selected. Meeting a voltage and current rating is only the starting point. Designers must also consider what happens during startup, normal switching, maintenance, and abnormal conditions, as well as how the component will perform after years of operation. Progress in energy storage will depend not only on batteries and power conversion, but also on the components that connect, isolate, and control power throughout the system.
Higher Voltage Brings New Component Challenges
One of the clearest energy storage trends is the move toward higher-voltage and higher-power architectures. At a basic level, increasing voltage allows a system to deliver the same power with less current. This can help reduce conductive losses and the amount of copper required in parts of the system, supporting greater efficiency and more compact equipment.
However, higher voltage also makes component selection more challenging. Insulation, creepage and clearance distances, terminal design, heat dissipation, and DC arc control all become more important. These considerations apply across the electrical path, including busbars, connectors, fuses, switching devices, sensors, and the power conversion system.
In other words, the trend is not simply toward components with higher ratings. The components also need to provide dependable isolation and thermal performance while fitting into equipment that is becoming increasingly space constrained.
Reliable DC Switching Becomes More Important
Energy storage systems need a controlled way to connect and disconnect the batteries from the rest of the power path. This is where high-power relays and contactors can play an important role. Depending on the system architecture, they may be used for main switching, service isolation, or other controlled switching functions.
Not every relay in the system has the same job. Main relays carry the normal operating current and create the primary connection to the battery. A separate pre-charge relay may handle the lower-current startup path, while auxiliary contacts or other feedback can tell the controls whether a switching device has actually changed state. Looking at these functions separately helps designers choose the right device for each task instead of expecting one component to do everything.
DC switching is especially demanding because direct current does not naturally pass through zero every cycle the way alternating current does. When contacts open, the resulting DC arc can therefore be more difficult to extinguish. The contact structure, arc-control method, insulation, terminals, and thermal design all have to work together to achieve reliable switching.
Startup also needs to be managed carefully. Energy storage systems commonly connect to equipment containing DC-link capacitors. If the main switching device closes before those capacitors are charged in a controlled way, the inrush current can place unnecessary stress on contacts and other components. A pre-charge circuit creates a controlled current path before the main connection is completed. A pre-charge relay, used together with a resistor and the system controls, can help limit that initial current and create a more predictable startup sequence.
Selecting a high-power relay also involves more than comparing the largest voltage and current numbers on a datasheet. Designers need to consider the continuous current the relay will carry, the conditions it must actually make or break, how often it will switch, the expected service life, and the temperature inside the enclosure. Coil power, mounting, terminals, control voltage, and available feedback can also affect the surrounding design. A relay that fits the electrical requirement but creates extra heat, wiring, or control complexity may not be the best choice for the complete system.
It is also important to separate switching from overcurrent protection. High-power relays do not replace fuses, circuit breakers, or other dedicated protective devices. They are one part of a coordinated design in which the switching device, protection, control logic, and feedback mechanisms all need to work together.
Compact Does Not Only Mean Physically Smaller
Higher power density is pushing manufacturers to fit more capability into less space. However, a physically smaller component does not automatically create a better or more compact system. If it generates too much heat, requires complicated wiring, or cannot maintain performance across the required operating range, it may create new design challenges elsewhere.
1. Typical pre-charge and main-relay switching sequence used to limit inrush current during system startup. Courtesy: Aratas America
The total design footprint matters. Power consumption, current paths, heat dissipation, terminal arrangements, and feedback functions can all affect enclosure size, cooling needs, assembly time, and long-term reliability. Auxiliary contacts, for example, can confirm switching status to the control system without requiring a completely separate method for that function.
The operating environment must also be considered. Storage systems may operate for years while experiencing repeated charge and discharge cycles, temperature changes, vibration, dust, humidity, and different installation altitudes. Component selection should reflect the real electrical load, switching frequency, ambient conditions, and maintenance strategy, not only an ideal rating on a datasheet.
Safety, Reliability Come from the Complete System
An important point is that no single component makes an energy storage system safe or reliable. These are system-level outcomes. UL 9540, for example, evaluates an energy storage system as a complete assembly and addresses charging, discharging, protection, control, and communication. A component rating or certification can support the design, but it does not prove that the complete system will operate safely.
The most valuable component innovations are therefore the ones that make safe operation easier to design, verify, and maintain. This includes dependable isolation, controlled switching, clear status feedback, manageable thermal performance, and operation suited to the intended environment. Designers also need to define how the components interact during startup, shutdown, maintenance, and fault response rather than evaluating each one by itself.
Component Innovation Will Help Enable Next Generation of ESS
Energy storage systems will continue to increase in capability while becoming more compact and integrated. Reaching those goals will require progress across batteries, power electronics, software, thermal management, and the components that carry and control power between them.
High-power relays and other switching technologies are one part of that progress. They may not be the most visible part of an energy storage system, but they directly affect how the system starts, stops, isolates, and operates over time. As the industry moves toward higher voltage and greater power density, thoughtful component selection and coordination will be essential for building energy storage systems that are safe, reliable, and scalable.
—Javi Tiggelaar is Business Development Associate for the Energy Industry at Aratas Americas .

source_document.body:
For years, virtual power plants (VPPs) were treated by much of the power industry as a promising but niche experiment. A way to aggregate a modest pool of rooftop solar and residential resources and call it a grid resource.
T hat framing no longer holds. In 2025 and through 2026, VPPs have moved much further into the mainstream of grid planning, and the resources they aggregate, the technology stack behind them, and the operators relying on them have all changed considerably.
COMMENTARY
For utilities and grid operators managing rising demand alongside a rapidly decentralizing generation mix, that shift matters. VPPs are no longer a bolt-on pilot program; they are becoming a genuine flexibility resource that needs to be planned early, dispatched, and integrated alongside any other asset on the system.
The first generation of (residential) VPPs drew almost entirely on rooftop solar and, later, paired with other home resources. That pool has broadened considerably. Managed EV charging providers are partnering with established rooftop solar aggregators and smart energy ecosystem providers, bringing charging infrastructure and the vehicles themselves into the resource mix alongside photovoltaics.
Battery energy storage systems (BESS), now a fast-growing distributed energy resource (DER) category in their own right, are developing in parallel and increasingly feeding directly into VPP portfolios. Sunrun, Tesla Energy, and Renew Home recently announced a partnership to aggregate more than 16 GW of residential batteries and smart thermostats. This project uses OpenADR 2.0b to communicate demand response signals and will sell capacity directly to hyperscale data center operators.
Commercial building management is following a similar trend. After playing a central role in the growth of utility demand response programs roughly two decades ago, the category is experiencing a new boost, driven by tighter integration between grid-interactive efficient buildings and utility operations. Modern implementations typically involve an edge gateway installed in a building’s server room (and the cloud), connected to the controls network, that identifies every device on standard building operational technology, or OT, protocols such as BACnet and Modbus. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted classification then builds a data model with granularity down to one- to 15-minute intervals.
What makes this new generation of VPPs different from earlier deployments is the software layer. Advanced cloud-based platforms, combined with AI-driven forecasting and load balancing, are what allow a portfolio spanning solar, storage, EV charging, heat pumps, and commercial building loads to be monitored, forecast, and optimized as a single coordinated resource with bi-directional communication between and among components rather than one-way curtailment signals. This tightens up the systems for the grid operators.
For power generation and transmission and distribution professionals, this is an opportunity and a challenge. A VPP is only as useful as a grid resource as its ability to communicate reliably with the systems dispatching it. That is where open, interoperable standards do the essential work: ensuring that a signal sent by a utility or an independent system operator, or ISO, is understood the same way regardless of which vendor’s battery, thermostat, or charging station is on the receiving end. As the resource mix diversifies further, that interoperability becomes the difference between a VPP that scales at a reasonable price and one that remains a collection of incompatible pilots. Stranded assets are less of a concern in this case.
The market’s growth is being reinforced from multiple directions. Long-established solar panel manufacturers are adding storage to their portfolios and actively working out how to connect and communicate directly with utilities as grid resources rather than as behind-the-meter equipment alone. New entrants from Europe and Asia are bringing additional VPP and DER management approaches into the U.S. market. And regulatory requirements are playing their part too: California’s 2023 compensation rule changes for Community Choice Aggregators (CCAs), for example, have already prompted CCAs to explore how VPPs can create new value for the buildings they serve while supporting grid reliability.
Within our own membership at the OpenADR Alliance (utilities, device manufacturers, and providers of renewables and EV charging infrastructure), VPP companies are now surfacing more often, which is itself a reasonable sign for where the industry’s attention is heading.
For power generation and grid operations professionals, the practical takeaway is that VPPs deserve the same planning discipline as any other flexible capacity resource: clear visibility into what is being aggregated, confidence in the communication standards tying it together, and realistic expectations about dispatchability. The technology and the resource base have both matured well beyond the early rooftop-solar-and-battery model. The question for utilities now isn’t whether VPPs belong in the resource mix, but how quickly they can be integrated with the rigor the rest of the grid already requires.
—Rolf Bienert is technical and managing director of the OpenADR Alliance.

1969 Dodge Super Bee With Day-Two Sunroof Is a Sad One-of-None Field Find
11 photos
Photo: Auto Archaeology/YouTube
Introduced in 1968, the Super Bee was Dodge's entry-level muscle car. It was also largely similar to the Plymouth Road Runner. But while the latter became pretty popular, the Super Bee moved far fewer units. By the time it was discontinued in 1971, the Super Bee had sold about 56,000 units. For reference, Plymouth delivered over 170,000 Road Runners over the same period.
About half of these Super Bees were sold during the 1969 model year, when 27,800 customers left showrooms driving one. The Super Bee was available with three powerplants that year. The muscle car came standard with the 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, which was rated at 335 horsepower. The optional 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi, good for 425 horsepower, was still available.
The third powerplant was brand-new for 1969. I'm talking about the six-barrel version of the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB (also called the Six-Pack). Rated at 390 horsepower, it was part of the A12 package, which included heavy-duty components for drag racing.
The Hemi Super Bee saw daylight in only 166 units, while the Six-Pack engine found its way into 1,907 examples. The remaining 25,727 cars were ordered with the base 383-cubic-inch big-block V8. Some of these cars are still on the road today and pop up for sale at public auctions. Most of them, however, are still rotting away in junkyards and barns. The green example you see here is one of the unlucky ones.
Documented by Ryan Brutt of YouTube's "Auto Archaeology," this Mopar has been sitting in the same spot since the 1980s. And that spot is among the worst for a steel classic: a farm field. It usually comes with full exposure to the elements, moisture, and total neglect. Unfortunately, one owner also opted to sell many parts, so the Super Bee is a sad sight today.
Once a gorgeous F8 green muscle car, the Dodge is now covered in surface rust, and it's missing both the hood and the front grille assembly. The drivetrain was also removed, and the interior doesn't look better either. The latter still has some of its original features in place, but the floor panels are nearly gone. As a result, there's a tree growing through the cabin, and it has already extended beyond the roof.
Interestingly enough, this Super Bee also has a sunroof opening. As you may already know, golden-era muscle cars with sunroofs are quite rare . It was a brand-new option at the time, and sales were still low, often enough in two- or three-digit territory. But this Super Bee wasn't actually born with a sunroof.
1969 was the first year when Chrysler had the feature on the options list. However, it was only offered on the Charger that year. Only 391 units were ordered with one, including 131 R/T models. The sunroof option was extended to the Challenger in 1970 but didn't find its way onto the Super Bee until 1971. Only nine cars were ordered with it that year.
The cutout you see here is a day-two addition. It was probably added sometime in the mid-to-late-1970s, when sunroofs became popular, but the entire assembly is missing. Our host says that the car was drag-raced by a local guy, but there's no relevant info on that.
Is this Super Bee worth saving? Well, I'd say it still has a few usable components, including the door panels, the rear taillight panel, and maybe a few body elements. A restoration is a different story, though. This Mopar requires a six-figure investment at this point, and it's definitely not worth it relative to its market value. But it's still sad seeing it like this.

The deal includes $550 million upfront plus undisclosed contingent value rights that will be offered upon certain milestones and bring the total potential deal value to $1.15 billion, according to a Monday press release .

“After working together for more than two years, we also know there is a strong fit in how we work: science first, entrepreneurial and focused on patients,” argenx CEO Karen Massey said in a statement. “We want to preserve what has made UNP successful while bringing the strengths of both teams together.”
UNP’s team will continue to operate from Santa Cruz, California, which will become argenx’s peptide discovery hub. The existing company will continue to lead discovery work within argenx. The parent company will provide clinical development and commercialization expertise to advance the resulting medicines.
The drug discovery biotech rose from humble beginnings. UNP was founded in 2016, originally operating out of Chief Scientific Officer Joshua Schwochert’s garage. Led by Cameron Pye as CEO, the pair believed the industry was overlooking the therapeutic potential of macrocyclic peptides.

Earlier this year, Novartis offered $100 million upfront and up to $1.7 billion in milestones to develop new medicines for undruggable targets in cardiovascular disease. In 2024, Merck shelled out $220 million to work with UNP in oncology, and BridgeBio also has a long-term partnership with the biotech.
UNP raised $45 million in a series B financing in March, with Merck’s venture capital arm and argenx participating.
Argenx and UNP announced their initial partnership in July 2025 . While the upfront fee was not disclosed, the licensing deal included $1.5 billion in future milestones.

1970 Camaro RS SS Restoration Stalled 40 Years Ago, Late Owner's Wife Finally Takes It for a Spin
94 photos
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds
What’s in a moniker worn by a car that’s been built 55 years ago, entered a restoration 40 years ago, and takes its first drive since the mid-eighties in 2026? A lifetime of treasures, memories, nostalgia, and heartfelt gratitude for a man who is no longer with us. But his spirit is, etched in the car he was prone to bring back on the road. His wife now sees it running again, courtesy of Hagerty’s Driveway Finders.
Some automotive projects carry far more weight than simple sheet metal and cast iron, serving instead as rolling monuments to lifelong love and unfinished dreams. In the latest episode of Hagerty's Driveway Finds series, hosts Dustin Hallinan and John Brito took a three-hour joyride to rescue a 1970 Chevrolet Camaro RS/SS 350.
The bronze split-bumper coupe belonged to Cindy and her late husband, fondly called “Camaro” Larry. Larry purchased the second-generation pony car in the early 1980s, and the couple actually went on their very first date inside its black vinyl cabin.
Around 1985, he decided the factory 350-cubic-inch small-block V8 was getting tired and plucked it from the engine bay to build a stronger replacement. Life intervened – and kept sidelining the project for 40 years. Despite spending eight years rebuilding the motor, Larry passed away before completing his cherished project.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Arriving in dealerships on February 26, 1970, the redesigned second-generation Camaro dropped the convertible to become a sport coupe exclusively, reaching 124,901 units for the model year. Only 12,578 buyers settled for the base 155-horsepower 250-cube inline-six. The rest of buyers (112,323 of them) ordered V8s, starting with the 200-horsepower 307 V8 small-block and the 250-horsepower L65 350-incher two-barrel V8.
Meanwhile, the $572.95 Z28 package attracted 8,733 enthusiasts with its solid-lifter 360-horsepower LT1 350-cubic-inch V8. Transmission choices across the 1970 lineup spanned a standard 3-speed manual, a 2-speed Powerglide automatic, 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 350 or 400 automatics, and three Muncie 4-speed manual gearboxes in wide-ratio M20, close-ratio M21, or heavy-duty M22 Rock Crusher specifications.
To sharpen the coupe's European-inspired styling, 27,136 buyers ticked the box for the RPO Z22 Rally Sport package, an appearance upgrade priced at $168.55 that could be combined with any trim. That Z22 Rally Sport option replaced the standard full-width front bumper with twin split bumperettes flanking a recessed black grille framed in a resilient Endura urethane nose cone, alongside round inboard parking lamps, hideaway windshield wipers, and bright window moldings.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Meanwhile, 12,476 customers ordered the RPO Z27 Super Sport package for $289.65, which added power front disc brakes, a blacked-out grille, F70-14 white-letter tires on 14-by-7-inch wheels, hood insulation, and SS badging.
Under the hood, the base Super Sport engine was the L48 350 four-barrel V8 (also found in Larry's RS/SS), which featured a 10.25:1 compression ratio and a Rochester Quadrajet carburetor to deliver 300 horsepower at 4,800 rpm and 380 lb-ft of torque at 3,200 rpm. 10,012 car nuts went with the base SS powerhouse.
Buyers craving big-block muscle could upgrade the SS with a 402-cubic-inch big-block V8 (still badged as a 396; not to be confused with the 400-CID small-block V8), choosing either the 350-horsepower L34 for $152.75 (1,864 units) or the solid-lifter 375-horsepower L78 for $385.50 (600 copies).
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Working outside their familiar garage presented an immediate challenge for Dustin Hallinan and John Brito, who walked into a packed home workshop where they did not know where any tools or hardware were stored. The 1970 Camaro rested on a four-post lift beneath a thick layer of dust and a canvas cover buried under miscellaneous parts and spare trim pieces. Nearby sat the partially assembled V8 on a stand beside a fresh automatic transmission case.
Before turning a wrench, the duo investigated whether the powerplant on the stand was the coupe's factory-born heart. The block casting numbers and foundry date codes aligned with the production date stamped on the cowl trim tag, pointing toward an original drivetrain. Machine work during the rebuild had decked the block pad and ground away the stamped VIN derivative, but Hallinan later confirmed the automatic transmission bore the matching VIN.
Every summer, Larry and Cindy attended Hot August Nights and stopped by Summit Racing, where they admired a display motor dressed in bright orange and black. Determined to honor that exact vision, Brito masked the aluminum Edelbrock Performer RPM cylinder heads and sprayed the iron block and Chevrolet-script valve covers in vibrant orange. Meanwhile, Hallinan spent two hours wire-wheeling, sanding, and degreasing the empty engine bay before applying black paint.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds The next morning, Hallinan bypassed the factory resistance wire with a dedicated power feed to support a modern High Energy Ignition distributor. Brito poured five quarts of zinc-rich oil into the pan, sealed the black Edelbrock intake manifold, and bolted on the water pump, fuel pump, flex plate, and starter. After grinding minor clearance on the starter and priming the oil system to 60 psi using a dedicated tool, they set timing at 15 degrees.
With cast-iron exhaust manifolds bolted down using anti-seize compound (that Brito jokingly called Never-Seize), the pair indexed a brand-new torque converter into the transmission. They mated the bellhousing to the block, pre-installed the tricky transmission cooler lines, and blew out the chassis fuel line. In a poetic twist, the same red cherry picker that removed the engine 40 years ago lowered it back home.
Working underneath the lift, Hallinan marveled at how clean and rust-free the floorpans remained after four decades of indoor storage. When the first driveshaft proved too short, the guys sorted through Larry's stash of seven spare shafts out back and found the original unit. A new Brawler carburetor then suffered stripped threads from a galled aluminum fuel fitting, forcing Hallinan to salvage a donor bowl from a vintage Holley carburetor.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds After Hallinan transferred the fresh float, needle, seat, and accelerator pump into the replacement bowl and Brito installed the radiator, Cindy joined them for the initial fire-up. The small-block roared to life for the first time in 40 years, but an alarming metallic racket forced an immediate shutdown. Inspecting the exhaust collector revealed a missing intermediate pipe sleeve, which one of Larry's friends conveniently produced from his own parts stash.
Even with the exhaust sleeve installed, a loud knocking sound persisted throughout the mandatory 15-minute camshaft break-in run, during which an uncapped radiator erupted and flooded the shop floor. Pulling the driver-side valve cover and spark plugs showed zero internal damage, leaving the mechanics baffled overnight. The next morning, Brito unbolted the driver-side exhaust manifold and discovered the casting was striking the aftermarket cylinder head and an oversized head bolt.
Grinding clearance into the cast-iron manifold and stacking two thick exhaust gaskets completely eliminated the terrifying clatter, allowing the V8 to purr with a choppy camshaft lope and gear-driven timing whine. With the transmission shifting into gear on the lift, the team turned their attention to the dry rear brake reservoir. They replaced the seized rear wheel cylinders and rubber hoses, bled the brakes, and installed a fresh set of blue spark plug wires.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Cheered on by a gathering of Larry's friends and family, Hallinan backed the Camaro off the lift and onto public pavement for its first road test in 40 years. The fresh plug wires cured a minor ignition miss, and the coupe charged up a steep 45-degree neighborhood hill with effortless power steering and crisp shifts. In fact, the refurbished brakes grabbed so hard that they foiled Brito's celebratory burnout attempt.
After two-and-a-half days of intense wrenching, the crew bolted the sculpted hood back on, washed away 40 years of grime, and handed the keys to Cindy. Sliding behind the tilt steering wheel, she cruised the exact hometown streets she and Larry had prowled four decades ago. Calling the revival her final hurrah for her late husband, a beaming Cindy said she felt like she was in heaven right alongside him.
