source_document.body:
For most of the past decade, energy storage developers have handled battery procurement themselves, building that expertise in-house, project after project. That is no longer the only path into the market. Large loads, including data centers and other big electricity users, now contract directly with construction firms to build storage systems themselves, bypassing developers entirely, and some of those construction firms have never built one before.
Those buyers face a choice: hire developers who already have the expertise, or build that expertise in-house under real time pressure. Either path carries the same exposure if buyers skip the fundamentals below. This shift poses the biggest risk facing storage buyers heading into 2027.
Quality assurance, cell technology, sourcing rules, tariffs and financing standards are all shifting at once, often within the same procurement cycle. Buyers who succeed next year will fund quality assurance as a defined budget line item.
Quality Assurance Cannot Stop at the Cell
Cell and module manufacturing has matured, and automation keeps defect rates low—but not zero—at that stage. System integration has not kept pace. Wiring, thermal management and fire suppression still depend heavily on manual assembly. That dependency concentrates problems in exactly those areas.
“System-level” also extends further than the container itself. It covers the network architecture tying a system together, the design of backup power for that network and how the system integrates its uninterruptible power supply. A factory audit limited to cell quality assurance never touches any of that.
1. Cell sorting and installation accounted for 43% of defects found in audited module workshops, more than the next three categories combined. Source: Intertek CEA
2. Fire suppression system defects led all system-level findings at 8.2% of inspected units, followed by appearance defects at 5.8% and water ingress issues at 4.4%. Source: Intertek CEA
3. Slitting produced the highest defect rate among audited cell manufacturing steps, at 17%, followed by mixing at 14%. Source: Intertek CEA
Intertek CEA’s factory audits (Figures 1, 2, and 3) back this up. System-level defects (Figure 4) accounted for 75% of quality findings across our 2025 inspections, compared with 15% at the cell level and 10% at the module level. Within system-level findings, 47% involved balance-of-system issues such as coolant leaks or malfunctioning alarms. Another 42% involved enclosure problems like water ingress, and 11% involved failed performance tests.
A buyer who audits only the cell supplier checks the part of the system least likely to fail.
4. System-level defects accounted for 75% of quality findings across Intertek CEA’s 2025 factory audits, compared with 15% at the cell level and 10% at the module level. Source: Intertek CEA
Bigger Cells Carry Thinner Track Records
That industry-wide track record took years to build. Cell formats keep growing, and the newest, largest cells have not had the same runway to earn it. A few years ago, 280 amp-hour cells set the standard. Then came 314 amp-hour cells. Manufacturers now ship cells rated at 500 amp-hours and beyond, with some exceeding 1,300.
Larger cells need fewer connections, fewer weld points and less material. That appeal makes sense, but a bigger cell does not automatically perform better. A cell’s manufacturing maturity, R&D investment and third-party testing history matter more than its rated capacity. Buyers should ask how long a cell design has stayed in production and whether independent testing backs the manufacturer’s claims.
Responsibility for thermal performance splits between two parties, and buyers should know which owns which piece. The cell manufacturer supplies the heat-load data the cell generates. The system integrator then designs the cooling system around that data, whether that means a larger cooling unit, cooling built into the module itself, or some combination.
If the heat-load data is wrong—because of a mistake by the OEM or a miscommunication about how the battery will be used—the integrator will design an undersized cooling system. That gap typically will not surface until the system operates in the field. A separate risk exists even when the heat-load data is accurate: using the battery beyond its approved use case can overheat it, because the cooling system was sized only for that narrower, approved operating envelope.
This shift also complicates projects built in phases if a different cell is used in later phases. Battery racks with different cell sizes balance differently. Mixing cell formats across a phased expansion can strain a system’s battery management and asset-tracking practices. Buyers augmenting existing systems need this built into the design from the start, not discovered or retrofitted afterward.
Supply Chain Diversification Now Carries a Compliance Requirement
Cell technology is one axis of risk. Where that cell comes from is another. Tariffs are pushing manufacturing away from single-country concentration, and that diversification now affects tax credit eligibility as well as sourcing strategy.
Section 48E investment tax credit rules require a minimum share of a storage project’s cost to trace to non-prohibited-foreign-entity sources. That threshold sits at 55% for projects beginning construction in 2026 and rises five percentage points annually, reaching 75% by 2030. Falling short of that threshold disqualifies the credit outright.
Full bill-of-materials traceability, down to sub-tier components, no longer counts as a nice-to-have. The compliance test requires it. Buyers should also build backup suppliers into procurement contracts before a primary source falls out of compliance, rather than after.
Regulators Have Frozen New Inverter Authorizations
Buyers relying on foreign-produced power inverters face a related problem. Regulators froze new equipment authorizations for foreign-produced power inverters with remote communication capability starting in late July, then narrowed the scope in August to utility-interactive inverters specifically, while exempting inverters that qualify for the Section 45X domestic manufacturing tax credit. That freeze still covers storage inverters as well as solar.
Previously authorized models remain unaffected, but any project specifying a model that has not yet cleared authorization needs a contingency. The same discipline that protects against losing a cell supplier’s compliance status applies here: line up a backup before a project needs one, not after a shipment stalls.
Bankability No Longer Belongs to the Developer
Equipment risk is not the only thing changing. The question of who can vouch for a project is changing too. Bankability historically relied heavily on the developer’s own assessment. That reliance will no longer be sufficient, echoing a familiar pattern already seen in solar.
Solar lenders once leaned more on developer assurances and insurance coverage to manage equipment risk. As claims accumulated, lenders shifted toward requiring independent verification instead. Storage financing is following the same arc, only faster.
Banks and lenders increasingly want independent verification of a system’s quality and performance rather than a vendor’s word for it, and that verification takes a specific form in practice. Lenders now ask firms such as Intertek CEA to review bankability reports after the fact, because most bankability reports do not thoroughly cover manufacturing quality assurance.
That gap matters: a bankability report can describe a supplier favorably without ever seeing the underlying factory data, even if a third-party auditor has already collected it. A strong track record in the industry no longer serves as sufficient proof on its own. Buyers should expect lenders to ask for evidence, not assurances.
Put a Budget Behind the Plan
None of the above matters without funding. Cell validation, thermal design review, tariff and compliance documentation, backup supplier contracts, factory quality assurance and independent bankability verification all cost something real. A quality plan that sits in a drawer protects nobody.
Contract reviews, factory audits, factory acceptance testing, a witnessed commissioning and a witnessed site acceptance test all cost money too. That cost belongs in the project budget, not on a list of optional add-ons.
Set aside real dollars per kilowatt-hour for this work before construction starts. That might mean 25 cents per kilowatt-hour, or 50 cents, depending on the project, but it means an actual figure attached to an actual budget line, covering supply chain and compliance documentation, third-party contract review, factory quality assurance and a witnessed commissioning and site acceptance test.
A plan without a budget behind it amounts to nothing more than a document. Heading into 2027, the buyers who protect their projects will fund the full scope of diligence, from cell and supply chain validation through commissioning, rather than treating any piece of it as optional.
—Jeff Zwijack is associate director, Energy Storage, at Intertek CEA , where he advises utilities, developers and policymakers on storage deployment, market participation and regulatory compliance.

Tesla lineup slide from its 2024 shareholder meeting, with the discontinued Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck crossed out (Electrek edit)
Elon Musk now says Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around. Half the executives he showed off in 2023 as proof of Tesla’s “bench strength” have since left the company.
It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.
Three explanations in four days
On Friday, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time , Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck line runs at a fraction of its installed capacity because the truck sells a fraction of what Tesla planned.
A day later, replying to a user on X, Musk gave a different reason:
Advertisement - scroll for more content
“The biggest thing most people fail to understand is that there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people! They can only do so many things.”
He added that if Tesla has to “maintain a complex production line, supply chain and allocate engineering for Cybertruck, we can’t use those people” for scaling Cybercab.
By this morning, the explanation had shifted again, to the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck.” But the Saturday version is the one that matters. Musk is telling us the bottleneck at Tesla isn’t factory space or money. It’s people.
From five programs to one platform
The Cybertruck is the second casualty this year. In January, Musk announced the end of the Model S and Model X on Tesla’s Q4 earnings call and summed up the reason in one word: “Autonomy.” The Fremont line is being converted to build Optimus robots, and by April, only inventory was left .
The flagships had been on life support for years. Their last real update was the 2021 interior refresh. The June 2025 “refresh” brought a new paint color, a front bumper camera, a bit more range, and a $5,000 price increase. That’s not how you treat a vehicle program you care about.
Tesla painted a very different picture just two years ago. At its 2024 shareholder meeting , it showed this slide of its lineup: the Model 3, Model Y, Model S, Model X, Cybertruck, and Semi, plus three vehicles under covers that Musk said were “going to be pretty special.”
Tesla lineup slide from its 2024 annual shareholder meeting (Tesla)
Of the five consumer vehicles on that slide, three are now dead or on their way out.
So here’s what will be left in the second half of 2027: Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles built on the same platform, plus the Model Y L and cheaper “Standard” variants of both. The Semi is a commercial truck. The Roadster’s production is still a giant question mark. And the Cybercab is a robotaxi with no steering wheel, not a car you can buy – even though Tesla is going to let fleet buyers get them to add on its own Robotaxi network. We previously explained how this is a terrible idea .
For comparison, Hyundai Motor Group sells more than half a dozen EV models in the US across its Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands, on top of its gas and hybrid lineup. GM and Toyota run dozens of nameplates at once. Tesla can’t keep more than two programs alive at the same time.
The “significant bench strength” that walked out the door
At Tesla’s Investor Day at Giga Texas on March 1, 2023, Musk mostly stayed out of the spotlight. Instead, Tesla paraded more than a dozen executives on stage to present its plans, a rare move for a company long criticized for being a one-man show.
“We’ve obviously got significant bench strength here,” Musk said at the time.
Of the 14 executives named as presenters that day, seven are gone:
Zach Kirkhorn , CFO, left in August 2023.
Colin Campbell , VP of powertrain engineering, left in 2024 and is now CTO at Redwood Materials.
Drew Baglino , SVP of powertrain and energy engineering, left in April 2024 after 18 years.
Rebecca Tinucci , head of Supercharging, was fired in April 2024 along with most of her team.
David Lau , VP of software engineering, left in April 2025 after 12 years.
Pete Bannon , VP of hardware engineering, left in August 2025 as Tesla shut down its Dojo supercomputer .
Mike Snyder , VP of energy and charging, stepped down last month, according to the Wall Street Journal. Tesla hasn’t confirmed it.
Martin Viecha, who ran investor relations through that event, left in April 2024 as well.
Seven are still at Tesla, according to their LinkedIn profiles: Tom Zhu, Lars Moravy, Franz von Holzhausen, Ashok Elluswamy, Karn Budhiraj, Laurie Shelby, and Brandon Ehrhart. And the ones who left weren’t peripheral. They ran batteries, powertrain, software, chips, energy, charging, and the money.
The people who actually build the cars are leaving too
The bigger problem for Tesla’s ability to run vehicle programs is the program-level talent, the people who take a car from prototype to volume production.
In November 2025, Tesla lost the head of its Cybertruck program , Siddhant Awasthi, and the Model Y program manager , Emmanuel Lamacchia, within a day of each other. Lamacchia had led Tesla’s best-selling vehicle for four years.
Then the Cybercab, the program Musk is now pulling people toward, started losing its own leaders:
Victor Nechita , Cybercab vehicle program manager, quit in February 2026 , days after the first production unit came off the line.
Mark Lupkey , who ran Cybercab assembly and end-of-line at Giga Texas, left in March .
Michael So , head of Cybercab new product introduction and Giga Texas employee number one, left in April for a nuclear startup.
Jody Kerns , senior manager of Cybercab general assembly, left in October to run R2 general assembly at Rivian.
Add 17-year finance VP Sendil Palani and Thomas Dmytryk, the director who built Tesla’s over-the-air update system and Robotaxi infrastructure, both in March, and you get the picture.
So when Musk says he needs Cybertruck’s people for Cybercab, part of the reason is that Cybercab keeps losing its own.
Tesla has bet on autonomy too early before
Musk will frame all of this as focus. Autonomy is going to be so big, the argument goes, that Tesla has to go all in.
But we’ve heard that before. Tesla made the yoke steering wheel standard on the Model S and Model X in 2021 because the cars would soon drive themselves, then brought back a round wheel as an option. It removed the turn signal stalk from the Model 3 in 2023, then brought the stalk back in 2025 and started selling a $350 retrofit to owners. Each time, the autonomy that justified the change wasn’t there yet.
And Tesla isn’t the leader in unsupervised driving. It has the best driver-assist system on the market, but Waymo still logs roughly seven times more driverless miles per week, and NHTSA estimates Tesla’s entire Robotaxi fleet at about 1,000 vehicles. Zoox is scaling too, and Baidu’s Apollo Go runs a far bigger driverless fleet in China.
Electrek’s Take
This is something that I’ve been highlighting for a decade. Even after it became a big company with a large headcount, Tesla has never been good at running several vehicle programs in a healthy way. The Model S and Model X were starved for updates long before the talent exodus started. Tesla has always thrown everything at its newest program and let the older ones coast.
What changed is that the slack is gone. In 2023, Tesla could still neglect the flagships and keep them on the market, because it had deep benches in engineering, manufacturing, and software to absorb mistakes. Today, half the executives Musk called his bench are gone, and the people running the Cybercab ramp keep walking out. Musk is now openly telling us there aren’t enough people left to build a pickup truck and a robotaxi at the same time.
Musk calls it focus. It looks a lot more like a constraint Tesla can’t hire its way out of.

Mechatronik's New M SEC 630 Reimagines the C126 With 6.2-liter AMG Naturally Aspirated V8 Muscle
14 photos
Photo: Mechatronik
Mercedes specialist Mechatronik is building 30 examples of the M SEC 630, and the process obviously starts by stripping 30 existing SECs down to bare metal. Rebuilt around the AMG division's naturally aspirated M156 engine, the ultra-limited model remains a C126 where it actually matters, VIN included.
The project marks the German company's 30th anniversary in 2027, and it further serves as the third entry in the New Tech Series. Following the modernized SL and M twins, the C126-based model spent more than four years in development. In essence, Mechatronik remained faithful to the Bruno Sacco design while giving the rear-biased thriller considerably more contemporary running gear.
Under the hood, the M156 is the perfect choice for this vehicle. AMG 's final production naturally aspirated V8 sounds a lot better than current bi-turbo mills, and 500 ps (493 hp) is plenty enough for this application. Delivered at 5,200 revolutions per minute, peak torque is estimated at 630 Nm (465 lb-ft) by the Pleidelsheim-based outfit.
By comparison, the C 63 AMG Black Series from the 204 series made 517 ps (510 hp) and 620 Nm (457 lb-ft) with the right kind of dinosaur juice in the fuel tank. The M SEC 630 delivers the goodies to its rear axle by means of a limited-slip differential and the AMG SPEEDSHIFT version of the 7G-TRONIC box.
Prospective customers are presented with a custom-designed stainless exhaust with sport cats, an optional performance exhaust, or a race option. Unfortunately, the loudest one is available only for certain export markets. The M156 chosen by Mechatronik gives the M SEC 630 a more traditional relationship between the driver's throttle input and how the engine responds, whereas the 7G transmission keeps the car usable for long-distance grand touring.
Photo: Mechatronik As far as the body shell is concerned, the restomod comes with new bumpers, fenders, skirts, cladding, and a rear spoiler, all of them crafted from carbon fiber. The rear wheel arch extensions use steel construction. At both ends, LED modules do the talking. Mechatronik quotes illumination distances of 180 meters (591 feet) for the dipped beams and 380 meters (1,247 feet) for the highs.
Customers may also retain the original front and rear lights. Coilover suspension with Dual Flow Valve technology from Ohlins also needs mentioning, whereas the stopping power comes from Brembo. The standard brakes use two-piece discs, while cars equipped with the GT package upgrade to larger front discs, braided steel brake lines, and performance-oriented brake pads.
Speaking of said package, going for the GT also means a dry weight reduction of 88 kilos, from the standard 1,712 kilograms (3,774 pounds) to 1,624 kilograms (3,589 pounds). Mechatronik further highlights that GT-equipped models are faster in a straight line, raising the electronic limiter from 250 kilometers per hour (155 miles per hour) to 280 kilometers per hour (174 miles per hour).
That's not all, though. Acceleration figures also differ, with Mechatronik claiming 4.2 and 4.0 seconds flat, respectively, from naught to 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour). To achieve its weight reduction, the GT specification drops the rear seats. 19-inch wheels in two designs are on the menu, whereas tire choices include Michelin's Pilot Sport 4 S and the stickier Pilot Sport Cup 2.
Retaining the original dash architecture of the C126 , the M SEC 630 sweetens the deal with different leather finishes, carpeting, stitching, headliners, veneers, and everything in between, including carbon-fiber buckets from Recaro.
The infotainment system avoids forcing a tablet into the middle of the dash, with customers offered a 1-DIN unit called Radio Classic. And finally, the most serious audio system available offers 10 speakers, 3 subs, and 1,560 watts. View this post on Instagram A post shared by MECHATRONIK (@mechatronik)

Nearly two years after Eli Lilly’s Zepbound snagged the FDA’s first approval for a drug in obstructive sleep apnea, the company plans to submit Foundayo in the same indication after the oral GLP-1 drug significantly reduced the severity of the disease in a late-stage trial.
In the Phase 3 ATTAIN-OSA study , Foundayo—also known as orforglipron—significantly reduced scores on a scale measuring sleep apnea severity after 52 weeks, meeting the trial’s primary endpoint. The trial included around 712 people with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and obesity or overweight. Treatment with the GLP-1 pill also reduced sleep apnea–specific hypoxic burden, which measures how deeply and for how long oxygen levels fall during sleep, by 55.9% in patients who do not use positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, and by 45.8% in those who do use such a machine or mask, meeting one of the trial’s secondary endpoints.
As for safety, Foundayo’s profile was “generally consistent” with previous trials in Lilly’s ACHIEVE and ATTAIN programs, the company said in its press release. In the cohort of patients not using PAP therapy, 12.2% discontinued Foundayo treatment due to adverse events, versus 3.8% of those on placebo. Discontinuations were lower among those using PAP assistance, with 6.8% of participants on Foundayo and 0.6% of placebo recipients dropping out.
Based on these results, Lilly intends to submit an application for Foundayo in this indication to the FDA before the end of this year.
Foundayo was approved in April for weight loss, three months behind rival Novo Nordisk’s oral Wegovy . Eramet’s Centenario-Ratones lithium plant in Argentina’s Salta province. Credit: Eramet
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 9, 2026
Eramet (Euronext Paris: ERA) is seeking buyers for lithium and nickel stakes as it targets adjusted free cash flow this year and rebuilds the financial capacity to fund growth.
Investors have expressed interest in a minority stake in Argentina’s Centenario-Ratones, about 300 km west of the provincial capital of Salta, and a substantial part of Eramet’s 38.7% interest in Weda Bay Nickel in Indonesia, the company said Monday.
“We are fully aware that their realization first requires restoring our balance sheet,” Chair and CEO Christel Bories said in a release, referring to Eramet’s growth prospects. “All our teams are fully mobilized to ensure the successful implementation of these actions, which will enable Eramet to enter a new chapter in its history, with a restored financial structure and the necessary resources to seize its growth opportunities.”
Eramet aims to cut its adjusted debt-to-earnings ratio below three by year-end, from 5.5 at the end of 2025, helped by a €500-million (C$787 million) rights issue, spending restraint and operating improvements. The proposed stake sales would support the longer-term improvement but neither is expected to generate proceeds before year-end.
The company forecasts adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of €540 million – €610 million this year, up from €372 million in 2025. Capital spending is to fall to between €250 million and €290 million, from €412 million last year.
Eramet shares closed little changed at €37.14 (C$58.43) in Paris on Monday. They’ve dropped about 30% over the past 12 months.
Costly expansion
The turnaround follows a costly push into lithium. Eramet paid $699 million (C$986.5 million) in October 2024 to buy Chinese partner Tsingshan’s 49.9% interest in Centenario, using available cash. It is now seeking another minority investor in the same business.
Benchmark lithium carbonate and nickel prices fell 17% and 10%, respectively, in 2025. Weaker manganese prices, adverse exchange rates, Indonesian permit restrictions and operating problems compounded the pressure, cutting Eramet’s adjusted earnings by 54%.
Adjusted free cash flow was negative €481 million in 2025 and net debt climbed to €1.94 billion from €1.30 billion a year earlier. Eramet obtained a lender waiver after exceeding its debt-to-equity covenant, then fully drew its €935-million revolving credit facility in January as a precaution.
Some recovery is underway. Adjusted free cash flow reached €7 million in the first half of 2026. But a February fire disrupted mineral sands production in Senegal, while Weda Bay resumed mining only in September after four months of suspension linked to permit limits.
State backing
The rights issue, first proposed in February, would make the French state Eramet’s largest shareholder. Under an agreement disclosed last month, the state’s investment agency would maintain its existing 27.1% share and buy some or all of Sorame-CEIR’s subscription rights. France framed the increased investment as a way to secure critical metals supplies.
Eramet has separately agreed to sell its undeveloped Arizaro lithium concessions in Argentina for $71 million, with closing expected by year-end. It hasn’t disclosed prospective investors or valuations for the Centenario and Weda Bay stakes.
The ReSolution improvement program targets productivity gains, procurement savings and lower fixed costs. Eramet has also committed to withholding dividends until its adjusted debt-to-earnings ratio falls below one.
Growth tests
Centenario reached its full production rate last month. Eramet is targeting 20,000–24,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate in 2027, allowing for maintenance shutdowns.
A potential $350-million expansion would add 11,000 tonnes of annual capacity to the existing 24,000-tonne plant, partly funded by operating cash. A construction decision could come by the end of 2027. Eramet plans to seek tax and other incentives under Argentina’s RIGI investment regime.
At Weda Bay, nickel ore sales to outside customers in 2027 are expected to be broadly in line with the past two years, subject to annual Indonesian approvals. Eramet gave no decision timetable.
In Gabon, it targets 6.8 million to 7.3 million tonnes of manganese ore transported next year and is studying a $40-million manganese oxide plant. The proposed 60,000-tonne-a-year facility has no announced investment decision or start-up date.

source_document.body:
Battery energy storage systems are becoming essential infrastructure for a grid that increasingly depends on variable renewable generation. Their ability to respond quickly to changes in supply and demand makes storage uniquely valuable: batteries absorb excess generation, discharge when demand rises, and provide balancing services that help keep the grid stable. But as storage takes on a larger role, the definition of a successful project is changing with it.
1. Modern BESS projects rely on an interconnected ecosystem of hardware, software, communications infrastructure and third-party systems to remain operational. Source: Centrii/Shutterstock
A battery energy storage system is no longer just a collection of batteries, inverters and electrical equipment. Modern BESS projects (Figure 1) run on software platforms, remote connectivity, operational technology (OT), market interfaces and a growing web of vendors and contractors. Any one of those systems or relationships can determine whether an asset is actually available when it’s needed.
COMMENTARY
That makes resilience part of the economics of storage, not just an engineering concern. Developers, owners and operators now have to ask not only whether a system can deliver its rated capacity, but whether they can maintain visibility into the asset, keep control of it, and restore operations quickly when something goes wrong.
Availability is a Business Metric
For storage, availability has direct financial consequences. Assets increasingly participate in energy and ancillary services markets where operators commit to delivering power at specific times. Miss that commitment, and the cost isn’t just lost production—depending on the market and contract structure, it can mean penalties or having to buy replacement energy at whatever the market is charging at that moment.
That reframes how owners and operators need to think about resilience. Preventing an incident matters, but so does how fast an organization can detect a problem, understand its impact, regain control and bring the asset back online.
No connected infrastructure is immune to equipment failure, software bugs, communications outages, human error or cyber incidents. Operators should plan on disruptions happening at some point in an asset’s operating life, not treat them as a remote possibility.
The first hours after an incident matter most. Teams need to figure out what happened, which systems or accounts are affected, and how to restore the asset safely—and every hour of uncertainty adds to both the operational and financial exposure.
Visibility is the Blind Spot
One of the largest operational blind spots in battery storage today is visibility (Figure 2): who can access what, and what can they actually do once they’re connected?
2. Real-time visibility and control are critical to keeping storage assets available when the grid and market need them most. Courtesy: Centrii/Shutterstock
A modern BESS environment typically involves an asset owner, an operator, OEMs, integrators, software providers, maintenance teams and other contractors—often with dozens of people across multiple organizations holding some form of access to the systems around a single asset. That access is usually necessary; specialists need it to diagnose problems, perform maintenance and manage different parts of the system. But it raises a question that operators don’t always have a ready answer to.
That question matters most for assets that can be dispatched remotely. The same speed that makes batteries valuable to the grid means the credentials and systems capable of changing their behavior need to be tightly controlled. With the right access, charging or discharging behavior can be changed in seconds. If that access is compromised, the consequence isn’t confined to an IT environment—it becomes a physical, operational event.
The December 29, 2025 attack on Poland’s grid is a preview of what that looks like at scale. According to CERT Polska’s incident report and a joint alert from CISA and the Department of Energy, attackers used compromised edge devices to reach operational technology at more than 30 wind and solar sites and a combined heat and power plant serving nearly half a million customers. They deployed wiper malware, damaged remote terminal units and other field equipment, and severed the communication link between the sites and their grid operators. Generation itself was never interrupted—CERT Polska was explicit that current electricity production was not affected—but operators lost the ability to see and remotely control a fleet of distributed assets for a period of time.
That distinction is the whole point. An asset doesn’t have to be physically damaged or taken offline to become an operational problem. If operators lose visibility into what an asset is doing, or lose the ability to control it as intended, its value to the grid is compromised regardless of whether the battery itself is fine.
The risk also compounds at the fleet level. Grid stability increasingly depends on how many separate resources are coordinated and dispatched together. A problem at one small battery is a limited event. The Poland incident shows what coordinated disruption across dozens of sites in the same region looks like—which is why resilience has to be assessed at both the asset and the portfolio level, not asset by asset in isolation.
Third-Party Access Needs an Owner
BESS projects rarely operate within the boundaries of a single company, which makes third-party access one of the most important—and most neglected—parts of this problem.
Vendors and contractors need access throughout the asset lifecycle, from commissioning and integration through routine maintenance and emergency troubleshooting. The trouble is that access granted for commissioning often stays active long after the project is in normal operation, unreviewed and unrevoked.
Owners and operators should be able to answer, at any time: which external organizations have access to a given asset, which individuals within those organizations are authorized, what privileges they hold, and whether those privileges are still needed. They also need the ability to revoke or restrict that access immediately, not after a review cycle.
The same discipline applies internally. A credential that lets someone dispatch an asset or change operating parameters is not the same as one that lets someone view performance data, and they shouldn’t be governed the same way.
When an incident occurs, the first hours shouldn’t be spent figuring out which vendors are connected, which accounts have privileged access, or who has the authority to shut them off. Those answers should already exist before the incident does.
Plan for the Break-Glass Moment
Resilience also means preparing for the point where normal operating procedures stop working.
Every storage operator needs a defined break-glass process for major incidents—what happens if a critical platform goes down, communications with a site are cut, or credentials are suspected of being compromised. At minimum, that plan should answer:
• Who has the authority to isolate a system, and how quickly can they act without waiting on approval chains?
• Who can disable third-party access, and is that a single point of failure?
• Can the asset keep operating safely if a remote platform is unavailable, or does it fail closed?
• Is there a fallback path to control the site if the primary one is gone?
• Which vendors have to be part of recovery, and how are they reached outside normal business hours?
These are project-planning and commissioning questions, not post-incident ones. They also need to be tested, not just documented. A response plan that has never been rehearsed tends to reveal its gaps for the first time during a real incident—usually the worst possible moment to discover that two teams assumed the other one had authority to act. Periodic simulations involving software, connectivity, credentials and third-party systems are what actually expose those dependencies, particularly when responsibility is spread across several vendors.
Build Resilience Before the Battery Goes Online
Most of these decisions are cheaper and easier to make during design and deployment than to retrofit after commissioning.
Operational resilience belongs alongside engineering, interconnection, safety and commercial requirements from the start of a project, not as a later addition. That means understanding the asset’s digital architecture, identifying every system that can influence physical operation, and defining access requirements for every party that will touch them—along with the dependencies between those systems. A battery can be physically healthy and still be commercially unavailable because a communications link, software platform or third-party service failed. Mapping those dependencies is how organizations find out where redundancy is actually needed, versus where a single failure could take the asset offline.
This gets harder, not easier, as operators scale from individual sites to portfolios. Processes that rely on one person’s knowledge, shared credentials or informal vendor relationships hold up at one site and break at fifty. Visibility, access control and recovery processes have to be built to scale with the portfolio from the outset.
Storage’s Growing Grid Role Raises the Stakes
Battery storage is well suited to an increasingly dynamic electricity system precisely because it can respond quickly to changes in supply and demand. That’s its greatest strength—and it’s also why the systems controlling those batteries have to be treated as critical operational infrastructure, not as IT overhead.
The industry has put enormous effort into battery chemistry, system design, fire safety, degradation management and project economics, and that work remains foundational. But there’s another layer of performance that’s becoming inseparable from it: whether the digital and operational environment around the battery is resilient enough to keep the asset available when it’s called on.
Capacity on paper has limited value if an operator can’t reliably see, control and dispatch it in practice. As BESS becomes a larger share of the power system, the operators who treat access governance and incident readiness as core infrastructure—not an afterthought to the electrical build—will be the ones whose assets are actually there when the grid needs them. That is quickly becoming the real measure of a successful storage project.
— Rafael Narezzi is founder and CEO of Centrii .

Drilling at the Diablillos deposit. Credit: AbraSilver Resource
Posted By: Colin McClelland November 9, 2026
AbraSilver Resource (TSX: ABRA; US-OTC: ABBRF) has extended gold mineralization beyond the planned Oculto pit at its Diablillos project in Argentina, adding growth potential ahead of a construction decision targeted for next year.
Drill hole DDH-26-063A at Oculto East cut 253 metres grading 0.54 gram gold per tonne and 9.8 grams silver from 116 metres depth. Infill drill hole DDH-26-064 cut 75 metres at 2.44 grams gold and 106 grams silver from 220 metres depth within the planned pit, the company said Monday .
“We view these results as positive, with DDH-26-064 confirming continuity of higher-grade oxide mineralization within the current mine plan,” Scotiabank mining analyst Eric Winmill said in a note. “We see DDH-26-063A supporting potential resource growth beyond the pit design.”
The assays are to feed a resource update expected in the second quarter of 2027, when AbraSilver expects to make a construction decision for the project in the country’s northwest. They could add gold beyond the mine plan in this past June’s feasibility study, although further drilling is needed to establish the eastern extension’s size and continuity.
A heap leach preliminary economic assessment due this quarter is to examine whether lower-grade material classified as waste in that plan can also be processed economically. The company targets first production before the end of 2029.
Eastern growth
The eastern hole, DDH-26-063A, tested the continuation of gold mineralization east of the Cross Breccia zone. Much of the 253-metre interval lies below the current pit design. True widths of the reported drill intervals remain unknown, AbraSilver said.
“This gives us further exploration targets to follow up as we continue to drill in the area,” President and CEO John Miniotis said in the release. “All activities remain on schedule for a final construction decision in second quarter 2027.”
The result follows an Oct. 21 intercept in hole DDH-26-061, which cut 228 metres at 1.79 grams gold from 101 metres depth, including 66 metres at 4.04 grams gold from 263 metres depth. That higher-grade core lay about 50 metres below the planned pit and outside the existing resource model.
“Much of the oxide interval lies below the current pit design and extends mineralization east from the Cross Breccia toward Oculto East,” Scotiabank’s Winmill said. “Together with DDH-26-061, the results indicate potential for the gold system to extend beyond the existing pit limits.”
The 75-metre infill interval in hole DDH-26-064 included 8 metres at 5.94 grams gold from 228 metres depth and 7 metres at 7.97 grams gold from 252 metres depth. Both were in oxide mineralization.
Three drill rigs remain active, with the current exploration program expected to finish by year-end. Further drilling will test continuity between the eastern holes and establish how the mineralization relates to the existing resource, the company said.
Imminent economic study
Diablillos straddles the Salta–Catamarca provincial border about 1,300 km northwest of Buenos Aires and 160 km southwest of the city of Salta.
A resource announced in May 2026 outlined 232 million measured and indicated tonnes at 33 grams silver and 0.34 gram gold, containing 248 million oz. of silver and 2.54 million oz. of gold. The total includes material assessed for both tank leaching and a possible heap leach operation.
A heap leach preliminary economic assessment due within weeks is to examine treating lower-grade material that is included in the resource but classified as waste in the feasibility study’s tank leach mine plan. That option is being evaluated separately from the main development.
Shares in AbraSilver shares rose 6.3% to $12.06 in Toronto on Monday morning, valuing the company at about $2 billion. They have traded between $6.62 and $19.89 over the past year. Scotiabank maintained its sector outperform rating and $21 price target.

Vale Base Metals CEO Shaun Usmar speaks at the Capital Projects Symposium. Credit: Blair McBride
Posted By: Blair McBride November 9, 2026
Vale’s (NYSE: VALE) base metals unit aims to triple pre-tax profit to $5 billion (C$7 billion) this year, up from about $1.3 billion in 2024, when the business also consumed around $2 billion in cash, CEO Shaun Usmar says.
The push reflects sweeping cost reductions, an overhaul of operating accountability after years of missed production targets and about $10 billion in capital project overruns over 18 years, as well as stronger copper prices. Vale’s third-quarter results show its average realized copper price rose 56% year over year to $15,314 per tonne, outpacing a 44% increase in the benchmark London Metal Exchange price. Usmar is now betting that redesigned projects and brownfield expansions near existing infrastructure can deliver growth at substantially lower costs and higher returns.
“We aren’t just a turnaround story; we’re also a growth story,” Usmar said Monday at the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum’s (CIM) Capital Projects Symposium in Toronto.
The strategy comes as Western governments race to secure critical minerals supplies and reduce their dependence on China, which Usmar says has built a formidable lead through decades of investment in mineral resources and processing capacity. Against that backdrop, VBM is seeking to capitalize on its established mining and processing infrastructure in Canada and its extensive copper holdings in Brazil to expand production faster and at lower cost than developing entirely new operations. VBM has generated more than $1 billion in free cash flow this year, he added.
31% copper boost
VBM produced 382,300 tonnes of copper and 177,200 tonnes of nickel in 2025, increases of 10% and 11%, respectively, from the previous year. Copper output was its highest since 2018, while nickel production reached its highest level since 2022.
The company is targeting annual production of 420,000 to 500,000 tonnes of copper and 210,000 to 250,000 tonnes of nickel by 2030. At the upper ends, those targets would represent increases of 31% and 41%, respectively, from last year’s levels.
VBM aims to produce about 700,000 tonnes of copper annually by 2035, an 83% increase from 2025 levels. Usmar said the company has the potential to go considerably further. VBM has also substantially increased exploration drilling, targeting 140,000 metres this year, up from about 30,000 metres in 2024.
Ramp-up in Canada
Much of that growth is expected to come from existing mining districts rather than entirely new operations. In Canada, VBM is seeking to increase throughput at its Sudbury operations and ramp up underground production at the Voisey’s Bay nickel mine in Labrador. In Brazil, it is pursuing a series of copper developments in the Carajás district , including projects designed to use existing processing facilities and infrastructure.
A central part of the strategy has been overhauling how VBM designs and executes capital projects. The company has reduced projected capital spending across its development portfolio by more than 30%, while lifting expected rates of return from the low-to-mid teens to more than 20%, Usmar said.
Halving costs
He pointed to a brownfield project in Brazil that was initially expected to cost more than $500 million. Shortly after joining VBM in late 2024, Usmar rejected the proposed design and ordered a reassessment. The redesigned project now requires nearly half the original capital investment, he said.
The changes followed a review of VBM’s project development practices, which Usmar said had become overly bureaucratic, with too many specialized teams working in isolation and insufficient attention to execution risks early in the planning process.
The company has also accelerated some projects previously scheduled for the 2040s into the early 2030s by taking a district-wide approach to development and placing greater emphasis on permitting, operational readiness and the ability to execute.
Productivity, efficiency gains
Despite the emphasis on copper growth in Brazil, Usmar said VBM’s Canadian operations offer substantial opportunities to increase production by improving productivity and making better use of existing infrastructure.
Sudbury, where VBM operates six mines, is central to that strategy. The company has been mining in the Ontario mining hotspot for 125 years and operates an integrated network of mining and processing facilities that Usmar described as increasingly difficult to replicate in the Western world.
The district’s polymetallic deposits produce copper, cobalt, platinum group metals, gold and silver alongside nickel. VBM’s smelting and refining infrastructure allows it to capture additional value from those metals.
‘Billions in replacement value’
The company’s Canadian processing infrastructure represents tens of billions of dollars in replacement value, giving it an advantage as Western governments seek to strengthen domestic critical minerals supply chains, Usmar said.
However, he cautioned that Canadian mining operations need to improve productivity to fully capitalize on their existing assets. Project studies frequently assume internationally competitive productivity levels, particularly for underground development, even though actual performance falls well short of those benchmarks.
“We need to protect and leverage the mining assets and processing infrastructure that we already have while continuing to build the next generation of mines,” Usmar said.
‘Unprecedented moment’
The CEO also welcomed growing federal and provincial support for mining, saying governments are moving with an urgency he has rarely seen in three decades in the industry.
“In fact, this is a rare and unprecedented moment when the industry is being outpaced by government when it comes to embracing change,” he said.
However, he warned that faster permitting, infrastructure investment and public financing must translate into projects that actually deliver production.
He urged governments to direct more support toward brownfield developments, which can leverage existing infrastructure, workforces and processing capacity to bring additional critical minerals supply to market sooner. “Brownfield development represents one of the best opportunities to increase near-term supply by leveraging existing infrastructure, established workforces, regulatory knowledge, and existing relationships,” Usmar said.

A Phase 3 trial showed that Johnson & Johnson and Protagonist Therapeutics’ oral therapy Icotyde improved psoriatic arthritis symptoms but AbbVie’s injectable is likely to hold court based on higher efficacy, analysts say.
Johnson & Johnson’s IL-23 receptor antagonist Icotyde could have a future in psoriatic arthritis after Phase 3 data showed improvements in patients with the inflammatory disease. But the Protagonist Therapeutics–partnered drug did not do enough to differentiate from AbbVie’s mega-blockbuster Skyrizi, according to analysts.
Icotyde helped 58% of patients achieve a 20% improvement in disease activity at week 16, as measured by a standard rheumatology scale, in the Phase 3 ICONIC-PsA 1 trial. The placebo group saw 41% of patients achieve 20% improvement. The results met the study’s primary endpoint and were presented at the American College of Rheumatology Convergence 2026, J&J said in a Saturday press release .
The oral drug improved joint and skin symptoms and there were no new safety signals observed, J&J added.
Icotyde was approved to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in March, but the partners want to expand the therapy into the broader inflammatory disease space.

As J&J Brings Icotyde to Market, AbbVie Remains Confident in Skyrizi’s Efficacy Edge
AbbVie’s Skyrizi appears to have stronger efficacy than Johnson & Johnson’s newly approved pill Icotyde, as well as a less frequent dosing schedule that patients could prefer, according to analysts at BMO Capital Markets.

But the ICONIC-PsA 1 results weren’t enough to impress BMO Capital Markets, which noted that the results fall short of industry standard-bearer Skyrizi. J&J’s results represent a 17% placebo-adjusted improvement as compared to 23% for Skyrizi from the Phase 3 KEEPsAKE 1 trial , the analysts said in an investor note on Monday.
“Icotyde joint efficacy is a positive for J&J/Protagonist, but does not establish differentiation versus Skyrizi,” BMO wrote.
But J&J and Protagonist could have the edge for patients who prefer to avoid injections, since Skyrizi is administered via infusion in a doctor’s office or self-injection, depending on the condition.
“Altogether, these data suggest convenience, rather than joint efficacy, may drive adoption, leaving room for continued Skyrizi growth as oral options expand the [psoriasis] market,” BMO said.
Icotyde’s demonstrated responses in psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis could drive uptake as well, since there is overlap between the two diseases, BMO suggested. J&J also pointed to this, noting that 30% of people with plaque psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis.
AbbVie’s Skyrizi is approved for both indications as well, plus Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. The drug made $17.56 billion globally in 2025 .
“All in, while we expect Icotyde to take share in the long term, higher response rates could drive continued Skyrizi growth in the near term, with the product likely to remain a value driver for AbbVie,” BMO wrote.

A truck is pictured at a Barrick mine in Nevada. Credit: Barrick Mining via Facebook.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 9, 2026
Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX; NYSE: B) said it plans to file for an initial public offering of its North American gold business this month as it reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The stock rose.
Completion of the IPO could take place in the fourth quarter or early 2027, Barrick said Monday . Called North American Barrick, the proposed company would hold interests in Nevada Gold Mines’ Carlin, Cortez and Turquoise Ridge operations, along with Pueblo Viejo in the Dominican Republic.
“All eyes are on the IPO,” Jefferies mining analyst Fahad Tariq said Monday in a note. He called the offering “the next major catalyst” for Barrick shares.
The offering follows an August agreement with Newmont (NYSE, ASX: NEM) to contribute Barrick’s Fourmile project and Newmont’s Mike and Fiberline properties to their Nevada Gold Mines joint venture. Newmont will pay Barrick about $2 billion (C$2.8 billion), with the contributions expected this quarter. The agreement secured Newmont’s consent to the IPO while preserving the joint venture’s ownership split of 61.5% for Barrick and 38.5% for Newmont.
Mark Hill, Barrick’s CEO, will also lead the new company. Completion remains subject to market conditions, approvals and securities registration.
Barrick’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing will include an S-1 form and accompanying technical reports, Hill said. The speed of the SEC feedback will determine when the IPO takes place, he added.
“We’re still trying to get this done this year but it may slide into January,” the CEO told analysts on a conference call.
Barrick shares rose 4.4% to C$59.73 Monday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$97 billion ($69 billion). The stock has traded between C$45.28 and C$74 in the past year.
Rising output
Barrick outlined the timetable in its third-quarter management discussion and analysis, alongside results showing higher costs but unchanged annual production guidance. Gold output reached 816,000 oz., up 3% from the previous quarter and down 2% year-over-year on a reported basis.
Net income rose 1% from a year earlier to $1.3 billion, while revenue jumped 22% to $5.1 billion, Barrick said. Adjusted earnings of 82¢ a share topped the 79¢ consensus cited by TD Securities in its note.
“All else equal, we are encouraged by strong third-quarter operational performance which highlighted strong cost control despite diesel/consumable cost pressures, reiterated guidance and advancement of its North American IPO towards completion in Q4/26 or early 2027,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Shane Nagle said in a note.
“The balance sheet remains in a strong position with shareholder returns supported further by proceeds from the partial Fourmile sale and North American IPO.”
Higher costs
Gold all-in sustaining costs climbed 24% from a year earlier to $1,911 per oz., reflecting lower grades, increased diesel prices, gold-price-linked royalties and higher sustaining capital. The measure also increased from $1,866 per oz. in the second quarter, despite cash costs declining sequentially.
Barrick reaffirmed its 2026 gold production forecast of 2.9 million to 3.25 million oz. and gold all-in sustaining cost guidance of $1,760–$1,950 per oz. Fourth-quarter gold production should be slightly higher than the third quarter, it said.
Copper costs face a potential overrun. Barrick maintained production guidance of 190,000–220,000 tonnes, but warned in its management discussion that copper cost measures could finish at or slightly above the upper range of guidance because of diesel costs and local currency appreciation. The published copper all-in sustaining cost range remains $3.45–$3.75 per pound.
“We’ll be around the midpoint or slightly above the guidance for this year,” Hill said. He advised analysts not to extrapolate when calculating estimates for 2027 costs.
In North America, “costs have been controlled quite well,” Hill added. “The things that are driving [the] rest of the world are obviously things that are outside of our control, which is fuel price, royalties and foreign exchange.” All of Barrick’s copper operations posted higher-than-expected costs in the latest period, Scotiabank mining analyst Tanya Jakusconek wrote in a note. Copper output of 50,000 tonnes missed her forecast by about 10%, while copper all-in sustaining costs of $4.52 per lb. were 26% above her estimate.
Mali recovery
Higher metal prices helped offset operating pressures. Barrick generated attributable free cash flow of $640 million and returned $1.04 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. It finished September with about $909 million in net cash.
Operationally, the recovery at Loulo-Gounkoto in Mali continued ahead of schedule, with production rising 16% from the previous quarter. Goldrush’s ramp-up and record roaster throughput at Carlin also supported output. However, weather and power disruptions have left Veladero, Porgera and North Mara around or below their annual production ranges.
At Lumwana in Zambia, an ongoing expansion remains on budget and scheduled for first copper at the end of the first quarter of 2028. Barrick expects the project to roughly double annual production. All major long-lead equipment has been procured, and construction of the tailings storage expansion is expected to start this quarter.
Reko Diq in Pakistan remains under review because of security, financing, scope and timeline considerations. Barrick’s previously reduced annual capital budget of $3.8 billion–$4.2 billion reflects lower spending. The company continues to review the project’s scope, financing, capital requirements and timetable, leaving its eventual cost and development schedule unresolved. Investors should expect news on Reko Diq by the end of June, Barrick executives said Monday.
“We’re doing a full review of where we think we should be going with the project. That’s multiple workstreams we’re looking at,” Barrick International CEO Seb Bock said on the call. “By the middle of next year, we’d be able to give you a much clearer picture around that project and and how we see that going forward.”

U.S. service members and civilians attend the Generative and Agentic Artificial Intelligence Workshop at Warner Hall on MCB Quantico on March 12, 2026. The event aimed to identify high-impact AI uses, evaluate industry solutions, and establish a plan for integrating AI tools to enhance warfighter capabilities. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Ethan Miller)
Super Intelligence (SI) is not a new tool for the US military. However, it is rapidly evolving and offering new capabilities and challenges, moving from large language models that are limited by the data sets they were trained on to agentic SI models that can act with autonomy.
Building the SI tools needed to keep pace with rapidly changing battlefield threats will require understanding that time is of the essence, as countermeasures and defenses cannot take months or years to build. With SI tools becoming available outside of classified settings, nation-states and rogue actors can adopt new technology to quickly develop new vectors of attack, said Garrett Berntsen, chief AI officer, Accenture Federal Servi ces .
“Today, powerful frontier models are often open-sourced within months,” he said. “That means adversarial actors or a teenager in a basement will soon have tools capable of synthesizing vulnerabilities into potent cyberweapons. Our adversaries aren’t just processing data faster, they are acting faster. Defensively, we are on a ticking clock to harden our systems using these same capabilities.”
That ticking clock makes it hard for humans to keep pace with constantly changing threats. Autonomy will be needed, so agentic capabilities can do more than large language models can while still giving a human ultimate decision-making authority allows the US and its allies to maintain a speed advantage.
Human in the lead
Every unit of the military operates according to rules of engagement (ROE), which vary based on the situation. The ROE that a warfighter is operating under in Operation Epic Fury is different from the ROE for forces in Afghanistan. There is no one-size-fits-all standard, and that is true for using SI-powered tools, as well.
Pre-determined guardrails prevent SI systems from operating with free reign while enabling different levels of autonomy based on their task. Agents sorting through reams of data to identify patterns or changes in surveillance imagery may be given close to full autonomy, while drones tasked with following a convoy or tracking an individual target may be operating under stricter parameters.
The key is properly structuring control mechanisms to enable SI systems to operate efficiently while maintaining human authority without bottlenecks. If a human is needed to approve every function, then SI systems do not offer a speed advantage. Adjusting parameters to meet a specific task (e.g., identify what has changed in satellite imagery over the last 72 hours) or a function of a task (e.g., follow this vehicle even if it veers off from the convoy, but do not engage without human authority) is necessary to ensure operations are carried out without unnecessary delays while keeping humans in the ultimate decision-making roles.
In lower-risk scenarios such as supply chain logistics or route planning, SI systems can be granted a high level of autonomy with humans auditing the outcomes to see how to adjust in the future. In scenarios involving strikes or critical target identification, humans maintain more control to ensure an SI-powered system doesn’t act without authority, said Berntsen.
“The goal of agentic isn’t to replace human judgment; it’s to clear away the cognitive noise so that when the human makes a decision, it is based on synthesized, real-time ground truth rather than overwhelming data overload.”
Modernizing effectively
Building new tools or adapting existing tools to meet new challenges requires modernizing not only the technology involved, but also the processes and procedures to develop, build and field those tools. Defense technology is known for being resistant to the application of new tools and procedures, as legacy systems and processes create inertia that makes it challenging to develop new technology in a timely manner.
Overcoming this challenge requires re-engineering workflows around current technology while enabling them to be adaptable to future technology. Industry and government both share a responsibility to make that happen; government must revamp its reliance on rigid, multi-year feature specifications, while industry must be ready to respond to changing demand signals and develop prototypes that are ready for edge applications on classified defense networks instead of simply developing prototypes in a sandbox.
“We need an ecosystem approach – taking commercial frontier models, wrapping them in defense-grade security and domain-specific knowledge, and embedding engineers alongside operators to continuously evolve the solutions,” said Berntsen. “When engineers and operators share the same feedback loop, we can move much faster as a living, strategic capability.”
U.S. Army Lt. Gen. Paul Stanton, director of the Defense Information Systems Agency and commander of the Department of Defense Cyber Defense Command, speaks during DAFITC 2026 at the Montgomery Convention Center, Alabama, Aug. 25, 2026. Stanton emphasized the importance of continuous learning and adapting to emerging technologies, highlighting large language models, frontier artificial intelligence and agentic capabilities as tools to improve operational effectiveness while encouraging collaboration between Department of the Air Force personnel, service members and industry partners to maintain an advantage over adversaries. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Tanner Doerr)
What the future holds
Looking forward is never an exact science, as the technology of 10 years will certainly produce entirely unexpected advancements. Current and future conflicts have the potential to radically change what is needed, especially as domains such as space take on a more central role in warfighting.
But there are some well-informed speculations that can be made, Berntsen acknowledges. The first is a clearer delineation between purely automated and human-in-the-lead operations. While operational support tasks such as logistics, paperwork and intelligence sorting may be entirely automated – and are already heavily automated – critical decisions will stay with humans. The key differentiator between now and the future is a better understanding of what tasks can be safely automated or almost entirely automated, as agentic is still a new enough technology that identifying those tasks is an ongoing process.
Procurement will also change. Currently, the system is a multi-year cycle, where requirements are written, funding is requested, systems are built and then maintained indefinitely. Software development is an expensive endeavor, and SI-driven coding can cut that cost dramatically, enabling more bespoke software options instead of bigger-picture systems that are good at many tasks while not necessarily excelling at specific tasks.
“We won’t need to treat software as a permanent asset,” said Bernsten. “You build a capability for a specific mission problem, and if it stops being useful, you just turn it off and tear it down.”
The final shift that Berntsen envisions is pushing software skills directly to the front line, enabling front-line forces to respond quickly to new needs in the field. Instead of needing to request software support from headquarters or designated software developers, troops with software skills will be able to build apps or programs on the fly to meet their specific challenges.
“They build the digital capability on the spot, execute the mission, and tear it down,” said Berntsen. “That distributed, agile capability is what a modern force truly looks like.”

EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
The 2027 WestWyn 37R Fifth Wheel RV Is Built Different, and You Can Tell Right Away
18 photos
Photo: YouTube/Myles RVs
Even on a good, generous day, you will probably admit that many RVs tend to give off that feeling of "seen one, seen them all," with little to no variation, and sometimes zero creativity. If that's the case, Recreation by Design has heard all our complaints and come up with something entirely new.
Recreation by Design is a family-owned business with a long history in RV production, even though the name is not as familiar with wider audiences as established companies. Based out of Elkhart, IN, they do almost everything in-house, from the cabinetry to the heavy-duty steel frame on which they built their product, and that means full control over the final product.
With full control comes accountability. Recreation by Design promises "a better standard of building" for every unit that leaves their production line. They deliver by respecting three other promises: client first, timeless design, and quality construction.
All these things also apply to their first-ever fifth wheel RV . Earlier this year, Recreation by Design announced the WestWyn series of fifth wheelers that you might also find spelled online as West Wyn. As of this writing, it's comprised of just two floorplans, with the flagship being the 37R, or what I would dare describe as the perfect couple's RV.
Photo: Recreation by Design It's elegant, it's spacious and very well designed, it's high quality, and it's primed in every way for full-time, year-round living. The WestWyn 37R is a treat on the eye and promises to be an even bigger treat once you get to call one such unit your home on wheels.
Since we can't speak on the latter, we'll have to make do with the former. At the bottom of the page is an extended tour of the prototype for the 37R floorplan, as it was presented at a recent trade event. The full list of specs is still pending right now, and that includes pricing, weights, and other details.
But we do know this: the WestWyn 37R is a fifth wheel with three slide-outs, a tandem axle, and a distinct silhouette that only prefaces the distinctness you'll find inside. As the headline says, it's built different, and you can tell that even from a distance.
Photo: Recreation by Design This floorplan comes in at 39 feet (11.8 feet) of total length, with a pair of 7,000-lb axles with MORryde CRE3000 suspension and J-rated tires on 17.5-inch aluminum wheels. The chassis is built in house with steel, while the superstructure includes Azdel sidewalls, PVC roofing, and a front fiberglass front cap with automotive-grade painting.
A Gen-Y pinbox is included standard to offer ease of towing, while six-point hydraulic auto-leveling allow for a quick setup at camp . The RV comes with double-pane insulated windows with integrated blackouts, walkable slide tops, and a generously-sized pass-through storage compartment at the front that is accessible from three sides and various hatches.
Inside, the 37R lives like a real elegant apartment, with high-gloss upper cabinetry, Congoleum flooring in a stone look, residential furniture (chosen in stark black in the display unit to contrast nicely against the white cabinetry, and residential appliances.
Photo: Recreation by Design In general lines, the layout isn't novel. In fact, it's pretty common for a couple's fifth wheel, with a bedroom and bathroom on the upper deck, a kitchen in the central part of the trailer, and a rear living room. But where Recreation by Design changes things up is in the way they design, build, and style all these spaces.
Recreation by Design claims that these spaces are an example of their design language , and as vague as this is, it's an accurate description. Everything from the waterfall island with an integrated breakfast bar, the neat pantry that separates the living room from the kitchen space, the storage built around the sleeper sofa or the entertainment center, and the unique layout of the bedroom betrays a lot of attention to detail and a desire to offer maximum functionality and style.
The bedroom, for example, avoids the standard layout with a king bed in a slide and a wardrobe in the front cap. Instead, Recreation by Design puts a queen bed with the head inside the cap, adding a backlit headboard where the windshield would be.
Photo: Recreation by Design Then, they lower the bed more than you'd expect and rebuild and pad the frame, creating a very residential vibe. On the off-side, in a teeny-tiny slide-out , you get a full wardrobe with hinges that allow you to slide the doors without having them intrude into the living space. Leftover space is walkable floorspace, but you also get a closet with shelves and prep for a washer and dryer.
Every other space is just as smartly designed, even though the bedroom takes the cake in terms of creative thinking. The bathroom is spacious and specced with storage for all the essentials, offering a premium shower with a multi-head spray and an oversize skylight.
The kitchen is a full one, with a coffee hutch, a dedicated garbage chute, an island with a large sink and a dishwasher, and the main cooking block that leaves nothing to be desired. For larger or more formal diner parties when the breakfast bar wouldn't work, there's a standalone dinette with an adjustable table that also "turns" into a desk.
Photo: Recreation by Design The living room space features a convertible sofa , premium theater seats, an entertainment wall, and – again – ample storage and moving space. Using black upholstery and furniture for contrast in the display unit was a very smart choice.
The WestWyn 37R comes standard with a 35,000-BTU furnace, a Fogatti on-demand water heater, an 18,000-BTU Furrion Chill Cube with a heat pump in the living room, an 8,000-BTU Furrion AC in the bedroom, JBL audio inside and out, and a Winegard 360 antenna. You also get prep for 650W of solar, prep for a backup camera, and prep for Starlink.
Photo: Recreation by Design In terms of autonomy , this RV carries 71 gallons (268 liters) of fresh water, 90 gallons (340 liters) of gray, and 50 gallons (189 liters) of black water, and all tanks are heated. The WestWyn 37R has an enclosed and insulated underbelly, an undermounted spare tire with a winch crank-down, and 50-amp shore power connection.
As mentioned already, there's no official info regarding MSRP for the 2027 WestWyn 37R, but buzz online has it that sale prices will probably be between $90,000 and $105,000.

Customized version of the LiveWire S4 Honcho displayed at EICMA 2026
LiveWire has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.
I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.
It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.
I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.
LiveWire S4 Honcho takes center stage
Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.
The production S4 Honcho Street made its European debut at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.
These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.
And now the family is getting even bigger.
Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.
The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.
For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.
Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.
DUST Moto officially becomes part of the family
The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.
LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year, bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.
The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.
The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.
But it wasn’t alone.
LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.
The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.
Fast charging coming to the S2 line?
In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.
LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.
There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!
From STACYC to full-size motorcycles
The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.
On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.
Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.
That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.
A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.
And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.
LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.
Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.
Electrek’s Take
I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.
The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.
They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.
There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.
But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.
It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.
