Vir Biotechnology is targeting a mid-2027 regulatory submission for its monthly chronic hepatitis delta regimen, with head-to-head data against Gilead’s Hepcludex expected next quarter.
Vir’s hepatitis delta combo tamps down virus as Gilead showdown looms
Vir Biotechnology is touting the potential curative value of its experimental chronic hepatitis delta combination after the regimen scored in a late-stage study, with close to half of patients achieving undetectable rates of the virus and normalized liver enzyme levels.
The biotech’s stock climbed 15% Monday morning following the announcement , rising from $12.21 at Friday close to $13.99 per share at time of publication.
The Phase 3 trial, dubbed Eclipse 1 , enrolled 124 patients with chronic hepatitis delta (CHD)—a severe and progressive viral liver infection. The open-label study randomized patients to receive monthly subcutaneous injections of the experimental siRNA therapy elebsiran and investigational monoclonal antibody tobevibart either immediately or delayed by three months, with the delayed group acting as a control.
Eclipse 1 hit its main goal, with 44% of patients who received elebsiran and tobevibart right away achieving undetectable rates of hepatitis delta virus (HDV) RNA and normal levels of the liver enzyme ALT at week 48. That’s compared to a 0% response rate in the delayed treatment group at week 12, according to Vir’s late-breaker presented yesterday at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases in Denver.
Safety was the study’s other primary endpoint, with Vir finding the regimen to be “well-tolerated with a favorable safety profile,” according to the company. One grade 3 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE) occurred when a patient experienced neutropenia, or low numbers of neutrophils in the blood; this safety event resolved in 15 days. The Phase 3 results help clarify the safety profile of Zealand and Boehringer Ingelheim’s survodutide, but analysts do not think the drug will find utility beyond patients with liver-related risk factors.
Zealand and Boehringer Ingelheim’s weight loss drug survodutide did not increase the risk of cardiovascular death in a highly anticipated late-stage trial, setting up global regulatory submissions for the weight loss therapy. But analysts were left unmoved by the safety profile, which showed the drug was non-inferior to placebo.
“While we believe survodutide will receive global regulatory approval, based on the totality of evidence to date, we expect its clinical use-case will likely be confined to patients living with elevated liver-related risk factors,” William Blair wrote Monday afternoon.
The results help clarify the safety profile of the drug, which analysts worried could spur heart-related side effects. Survodutide is a dual glucagon and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist. The mechanism of action has been associated with certain heart benefits, but early testing of the therapy has shown heart rate increases that drove discontinuations. The companies ran the Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT study to clarify the potential heart risks.
William Blair argued that the discontinuation concern remains after today’s readout and tolerability is a “significant liability” for the treatment.
“From a cardio protection perspective, survodutide established non-inferiority and demonstrated a numerical trend, though the trial was neither designed nor sufficiently powered to detect a superiority signal,” the analyst said.
The trial showed that survodutide did not increase the risk of major cardiovascular events, such as heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death of heart failure, as compared to placebo, according to a Monday press release . The study featured 5,530 adults who were overweight or living with obesity and have cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and/or at least two weight-related complications or risk factors.
The main goal of the massive trial was the time to occurrence of certain cardiovascular safety events, but there were also 27 secondary endpoints looking at blood pressure, waist circumference and change in body weight.
On the secondary endpoints, survodutide demonstrated a reduction in systolic blood pressure and waist circumference at 72 weeks versus placebo. The results were presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and published in The Lancet .

Unable to match rivals like Eli Lilly’s retatrutide on weight loss, Zealand and Boehringer have had to look to other measures to make a case for survodutide, according to Oppenheimer.
“We believe SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT is most important as a safety trial which can help establish whether glucagon-driven heart-rate elevation carries an arrhythmic or heart-failure cost, and we view any efficacy signal a secondary benefit,” the analysts wrote in a Nov. 3 note.

A service launched Nov. 9 promises to make donating excess inventory cheaper than destroying it by finding nonprofit recipients and arranging transportation . Vessel, the New York startup behind the service, also announced $5 million in seed funding led by HG Ventures.
What’s Related
The company says brands including Sol de Janeiro and Smashbox have already used it to donate more than $83 million in products to more than 5.5 million people. It reports keeping more than 2,000 tons of goods out of landfills or incineration while working before its public launch.
Vessel handles recipient screening, freight booking, shipment tracking and donation records. Brands approve the organizations receiving their products and use money already budgeted for destruction to pay for the service.
“We built Vessel so that brands no longer have to choose between doing what’s right for their business and what consumers expect,” said Teddy Raskin, Vessel’s co-founder and CEO.
It starts with a spreadsheet
Companies start by sending a spreadsheet or product list so Vessel can check what is suitable for donation. Its GoodOS software uses AI to assess more than 550,000 nonprofits across more than 160 million data points, then human reviewers review them before an organization earns Vessel Certified status.
Customers review the proposed recipients, approve the quote and prepare the goods for pickup. Vessel coordinates with the warehouse and receiving organizations, with records available through a dashboard.
Those records include bills of lading, signed proof of delivery and charity acknowledgment letters. Vessel says its standard nonprofit terms prohibit resale, and it puts product-use rules in writing before the customer approves a donation.
What the cost guarantee covers
According to Vessel’s website, qualifying inventory can be donated for at least 10% less than the customer’s total destruction cost. That comparison includes Vessel’s fees and freight and does not depend on tax savings.
Timing depends on the products, recipients’ ability to accept them, and freight availability. Vessel reviews those factors before confirming a plan.
Cheaper than destruction
Vessel says an unnamed medical distributor redirected more than 16 million syringes, totaling over 700 pallets , to more than 20 animal-care nonprofits across six states. The company said the project cost substantially less than destruction.
It also worked with an unnamed food and agricultural company to turn excess raw materials into more than 250,000 bars of soap for hygiene programs in Tanzania, Nepal and Madagascar. Money previously allocated for destruction paid for that project.
Flex Capital, Ford Street Ventures, and I2BF Global Ventures also participated in the seed round.

Your electric vehicle battery may last longer than you think. Ford says its EV batteries retain greater than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. Here are a few tips to keep yours healthy.
The Mustang Mach-E went on sale in late 2020 as Ford’s first fully electric crossover SUV designed from the ground up.
Since launching the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, Ford has been collecting data from over 36,000 vehicles that have traveled two billion miles across the US and Canada.
According to Ford, the Mach-E’s battery has retained 92% of its health on average over the past five years.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Across its full EV lineup, including the F-150 Lightning and E-Transit, Ford said its battery packs maintain more than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. The key number to look at is the spread, with 95% of vehicles falling between 87% and 97% health.
Of 2021 model-year EV owners, Ford said, more than 2,000 have crossed 100,000 miles with their original battery averaging better than 91% health, while over 30 have crossed the 200,000-mile mark and average 88% health.
Ford is using real-world data to help owners take good care of their electric vehicles, no matter how much they know about batteries and other EV tech.
It’s also applying lessons from developing the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, which will underpin its next-generation EVs, starting with the Fantom pickup next year.
How to maintain EV battery health over the long term
Ford offered a few simple, everyday tips to help owners support long-term battery health. For one, if possible, charge at home on Level 2 for daily commuting or driving and save DC fast charging for longer trips.
It also helps to avoid charging in extreme temperatures if you can. Preconditioning the battery can help bring it into the optimal temperature range, while parking in the shade on hot summer days can also help avoid long-term battery degradation.
Last, but not least, you can use the Ford App to find charge-level recommendations designed specifically for your vehicle and battery system.
The 2021 Mustang Mach-E uses an NCM battery, but some newer Ford batteries use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry, which is recommended to charge to 100% from time to time.
Ford Mustang Mach-E (left) and F-150 Lightning (right) (Source: Ford)
Ford has introduced new features in the Ford App to help owners maintain battery health specific to their vehicle and will continue to use the data to improve the experience as it introduces its next-gen EVs.
